#9990. Government may apply TV license fee to streaming services to fund the BBC

Controversial move could save the BBC by bringing in more than a billion in extra funding each year

A study suggests extending the TV license to cover streaming services such as YouTube and Netflix could solve the BBC’s funding problems, netting it an extra £1.6 billion ($2 billion) per year by 2032.

The British government is due to publish a white paper by the end of this year outlining its plans for the BBC's license fee and Royal Charter, which expires at the end of 2027.

One of the options is to extend the license so that it is needed to access streaming platforms like Netflix, Disney+, or Amazon Prime Video.

This is unlikely to prove popular, but if the fee was held at the current level (£180, $236 per year) it would generate up to £1.6 billion extra a year for the corporation and would better reflect how audiences watch television, according to entertainment industry research biz Ampere Analysis.

As any Brit knows, the BBC is funded primarily through the TV license, which is charged on a per household basis. A license is required to watch or record live TV on any broadcast channel, or access the BBC iPlayer for on-demand content. A license is not currently needed for on-demand streaming platforms.

The government is understood to believe the current license scheme is “outdated and no longer fit for purpose,” and is weighing several options to reform it. Scrapping it entirely looks unlikely for now: a committee found that other European countries that did so ended up with less stable funding for their public service broadcasters, and weaker independence from political interference.

TV licensing is controversial, with some people resenting having to pay the BBC just for the right to watch television. In response, the government has tried to limit fee increases, and made the license free for some elderly people. Together, these moved have reduced the BBC's funding, leading to service cuts and further. dissatisfaction.

Responding to a report by the National Audit Office (NAO) that found the BBC will remain under financial pressure despite widespread cuts, the National Union of Journalists (NUJ) urged the government to secure the broadcaster's future in the next charter renewal.

"The BBC shouldn't be in this position. These cuts are the result of a decade of underfunding, with NAO identifying a 26 percent real-terms reduction in license fee income in the last nine years alone," said NUJ general secretary Laura Davison.

Many Brits no longer pay the license fee, preferring to watch only streamed content, or claiming that they do. Ampere says more than 90 percent of UK households watch live television, but only 84 percent of eligible households pay the fee, meaning a sizable number are freeloading.  Extending the fee to cover on-demand and streaming services would close the loophole, it says.

Another option could see the license fee reduced to £150 ($196) in 2028, assuming perfect enforcement, analysts at Ampere say. They neglect to detail what this "perfect enforcement" mechanism consists of.

"Widening the remit of the license fee at current prices would significantly increase the BBC’s funding, strengthening its long-term financial position and ability to compete with local and global rivals," said Ampere Senior Analyst Sam Khoury.

"Alternatively, in the context of ongoing cost of living pressures in the UK, the government could opt to reduce the price of the fee payable by the extended pool of consumers. Coupled with a reformed enforcement mechanism that effectively reduces evasion, this would still improve the BBC's financial outlook relative to the status quo."

Earlier this year, the government revealed that it was planning for a switch-off of the broadcast digital terrestrial television (DTT) service in the future.

This is again because of the rapidly changing nature of the TV landscape, with viewers shifting to online streaming, creating a hybrid landscape between IPTV, traditional DTT, satellite broadcasting, and cable.

Current licenses for DTT services expire at the end of December, 2034, but the government may choose to extend them to 2044. ®

#9988. Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway: A fully-managed ingress solution for ECS services

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

When platform teams manage containerized applications at scale on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), configuring ingress networking for each service often becomes a bottleneck. For every new service, teams must provision and connect Application Load Balancers (ALBs), AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificates, AWS WAF web ACLs, and security groups, then keep those resources in sync as services scale, update, or operate. This per-service overhead slows down deployment velocity and increases the risk of configuration drift across an organization.

Today, we’re announcing Amazon ECS Gateway, a new account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account.

ECS Gateway introduces a clear separation of responsibilities between platform teams and application teams.

ECS Gateway offers host-based routing using ALBs and enables up to 25 services to share a single ALB, optimizing infrastructure costs. ECS manages the full lifecycle of the underlying infrastructure, provisioning the first ALB when your first service connects, adding more ALBs as capacity is reached, and removing them when no longer needed. Each service receives a unique DNS hostname, giving your teams a ready-to-use endpoint the moment provisioning completes.

A first look at ECS Gateway In the ECS console, platform team can create a gateway and sets its configuration. The infrastructure role is an IAM role that ECS assumes to provision and manage networking resources such as ALBs, security groups, and certificates in your account. To create a gateway, provide a gateway name and select an infrastructure role. You can optionally associate the gateway with ECS clusters during creation or later.

Choose a load balancing scheme, either public or VPC-internal traffic routing. Under Additional Settings, you can also set up a listener, port, maximum count of load balancers the gateway can scale to, and a web ACL lets you protect your web applications. Some settings, including the name, scheme, VPC, subnets, IP address type, listener protocol and port cannot be changed after gateway creation.

Using AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), call CreateGateway with a name (unique per account), an infrastructure role, and a configuration object. No infrastructure is provisioned until a service connects with a gateway connector.

Once the gateway is created, you can take a look at the detailed configuration, gateway routes, load balancers, and associated clusters.

Now associate the gateway with one or more clusters (many-to-many), to make it available to ECS services on those clusters.

Use AssociateGatewayWithCluster to make the gateway available to services on a cluster:

To create and manage the ECS Gateway programmatically, including calling APIs and searching documentation, try the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI coding tool. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Gateway documentation.

ECS Gateway:Behind the scenesA gateway can be associated with up to 10,000 clusters, and a single cluster supports up to five gateway associations. This many-to-many relationship gives platform teams the flexibility to share a gateway across environments or assign multiple gateways (for example, public and private) to a single cluster.

Platform teams can control access by choosing which gateways to associate with which clusters. For additional control, use IAM policies to restrict who can deploy services to specific clusters.

Application teams add the gateway connector to each service definition in CreateService or UpdateService. If you have an existing ECS service with its own load balancer, you can adopt ECS Gateway incrementally by calling UpdateService to add a gateway connector. Both ingress paths remain available, allowing you to validate the gateway connection before removing the existing load balancer configuration.

At deployment time, Amazon ECS evaluates the gateways associated with the cluster and connects the service to every compatible gateway. A gateway is compatible when its access type matches the service’s connector filter, it is in the same VPC as the service, and it covers all Availability Zones used by the service’s configured subnets.

For each connection, Amazon ECS assigns the service to an ALB with available capacity and provisions the per-service resources: an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, a listener rule routing traffic for that hostname to the service target group, and a service security group allowing inbound traffic only from the ALB security group. If no existing ALB has capacity, ECS creates a new one (up to maxAlbCount referring to quota limit). Once provisioning completes, the gateway route becomes ACTIVE, and the service URL is ready to receive traffic.

ECS Gateway handles common operational scenarios automatically:

Things to Know Here are a few important details to keep in mind:

Now available Amazon ECS Gateway is available now in all commercial AWS Regions where ECS is available at no additional charge. You pay only for the underlying infrastructure provisioned in your account when services connect to a gateway, including applicable ALB charges, CloudWatch logs and metrics, ACM certificates, and data transfer charges. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Pricing page.

To get started, create your first gateway today in the ECS console, and send feedback to AWS re:Post for ECS or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

Channy is a Lead Blogger of AWS News Blog and Principal Developer Advocate for AWS Cloud. As an open web enthusiast and blogger at heart, he loves community-driven learning and sharing of technology.

#9985. The world's fastest computers have a problem: Keeping the work running

I node what you did last summer: you went down when an HPC project was relying on you

Frontier, Oak Ridge National Laboratory's exascale supercomputer, has thousands of processors working together on scientific problems. It also has a surprisingly ordinary way of ruining a researcher's day: one node going down.

An uncorrectable memory error can do it, or a maintenance mishap. Scott Atchley, chief technology officer at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, describes technicians accidentally rebooting the wrong node or risking a neighboring node's power supply while working in tightly packed racks.

The hardware fault can affect just one node, but a simulation running across thousands of processors can grind to a halt. Then comes a series of questions. How recently did the application save its progress? How much computation needs repeating? And how long before the scheduler lets the job run again?

For operators, the challenge isn't just keeping the supercomputer running. It's keeping the science moving.

On Frontier, a memory error can have an outsized audience. Atchley says uncorrectable double-bit errors in high-bandwidth memory occurred about 1.5 times a day during the supercomputer's early bring-up.

Its predecessor, Summit, saw roughly one every two weeks. This sounds like a backward step, until you count the memory. Frontier has more than 16 times as much, giving bad bits considerably more places to hide.

Memory isn't the only problem. Problematic GPU firmware can crash a node, and so can a technician rebooting the wrong one. Interconnect faults add another way for a large job to come unstuck.

In a tightly coupled simulation using the Message Passing Interface (MPI) simulation, thousands of processes, or ranks, exchange data and participate in collective operations. If one rank disappears, the others cannot carry on as though nothing happened.

Clockwork.io CEO Suresh Vasudevan describes a similar dependency in synchronized GPU training.

One failed GPU can bring a 1,024-GPU job to a pause. An underperforming GPU can be almost as troublesome: if one participant runs at 80 percent speed, others might have to spend time waiting for it.

The bigger the machine, the more ways there are for one small problem to become everybody's problem.

Since stopping every component from failing isn't an option, researchers need a way to preserve their work. That's where checkpointing comes in. The application periodically saves its state so that, when something goes wrong, the simulation can resume from an earlier point instead of starting from scratch.

The catch is that saving progress costs computing time, and doing it too often can become almost as wasteful as losing the work itself.

Vasudevan explains this with an example. If writing a checkpoint takes 30 seconds, saving every five minutes consumes roughly 10 percent of computing time. Stretch that interval to 50 minutes, and the overhead drops to about 1 percent. But a failure could wipe out considerably more work.

Atchley says the calculation depends on the job's size and expected failure rate. He uses an example of ten-hour mean time between failures for a full machine job on Frontier. Using half the machine would roughly double that interval. The Young-Daly checkpointing model helps find the balance between saving too frequently and risking too much work.

Researchers also have the scheduler to contend with. Frontier's standard batch queue limits larger jobs to 12 hours, with shorter limits for smaller jobs. Its extended queue permits jobs of up to 64 nodes to run for 24 hours.

Then there's storage. Checkpoints can be written to the Lustre-based Orion filesystem or node-local SSDs. The faster the data can be saved, the less time checkpointing steals from the actual science.

Before recovery can begin, someone has to notice the job has stalled. Vasudevan says frameworks such as PyTorch can spend several minutes waiting before a hung process is recognized. Operators then have to sift through application logs and hardware telemetry to try to identify the offending GPU.

This can mean another encounter with the scheduler, which decides when replacement resources become available. Once allocated, the application still needs to load its libraries, initialize the runtime, and rebuild communication connections between processors.

And that's before the lost work enters the picture.

Restarting from a checkpoint means returning to the last saved state, potentially hours earlier, and repeating every calculation that has been completed since. The hardware may be back in action, but the simulation hasn't caught up.

Atchley says Frontier can launch a scheduled job in roughly 30 seconds. Restoring the application's data and getting back to useful computation takes longer.

Worse, researchers who lose their allocation may have to rejoin the queue. Depending on demand, Atchley says, "it might take me a day or so before my job runs again."

Keeping a supercomputer available is one thing. Making sure its processors are doing useful work is another, and the difference is measurable.

A 2026 study by researchers Carlo Graziani, Bethany Lusch, and Bronson Messer examined computational efficiency using records of 331,640 jobs run on Frontier during 2024. Their model estimated that, even with optimally timed checkpoints, only 95.7 percent of allocated computing resources would go toward useful calculations.

The remaining 4.3 percent? Around 1.2 percent goes to writing checkpoints, 2.8 percent disappears into failures, and another 0.3 percent is spent restarting applications.

Skipping checkpoints altogether would be worse. The model puts useful computation at just 91.4 percent without proactive checkpointing, demonstrating that saving work has a cost, but losing it can cost considerably more.

These efficiency figures are modeled estimates, not measurements of every source of lost productivity. They don't capture every delay from rejoining queues, stalled applications, or poorly performing components. The actual productivity bill can be harder to pin down.

This makes Frontier's reported 98.49 percent overall availability in 2024 an interesting contrast. The Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility's operational assessment measures how often the system was available to users.

Scale makes these losses expensive. An hour of wasted computation across 2,000 nodes represents 2,000 node hours gone, compared with just 100 node hours for a job using 100 nodes.

Saving checkpoints to local SSDs can speed things up, but there's a catch. If the node fails, the checkpoint stored on it can disappear too.

Atchley points to techniques such as Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory's Scalable Checkpoint/Restart (SCR), which can copy checkpoint data to neighboring nodes. This gives applications another recovery point if the original node goes down.

Keeping spare nodes available can also shorten recovery time. Atchley says researchers who reserve extra nodes will consume their computing allocation even if nothing breaks, which leaves fewer hours for useful computation.

Software developers are also trying to avoid the restart process altogether. Vasudevan describes techniques that attempt to transfer distributed application state to replacement hardware to allow synchronized workloads to continue without returning to an earlier checkpoint.

Some approaches can handle certain GPU and network failures through failover. These techniques depend on detecting faults quickly, preserving consistent application state, and having replacement resources available.

None of this makes failures disappear. Atchley notes that hardware improvements, including stronger memory protection, can address problems encountered on earlier machines. But as systems grow, new failure modes emerge.

The next generation of supercomputers may fix the faults that plagued their predecessors, but that doesn't mean they'll never break. Atchley explains that problems solved on one machine tend to give way to entirely new ones on the next.

Faster processors and more memory are only useful if scientists can keep their calculations moving. This makes fault detection and recovery every bit as important as another headline-grabbing performance record.

Resilience research, Atchley admits, "is not sexy at all." But when you're dealing with machines of this size, "scale just amplifies everything." ®

#9984. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities. AWS Continuum is a security service that finds and validates code vulnerabilities, then delivers fixes as patches you can automate or as pull requests in your repositories. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities confirms which findings are exploitable in your environment, ranks the resulting issues by business impact, and proposes a fix for each one. Every remediation starts in a mode where Continuum proposes the fix and a person approves it before it ships. In the future, you will be able to decide which actions Continuum can take on its own, within the guardrails you define.

Using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process. If your organization runs a large application estate, your scanners likely produce thousands of findings a day, and many of them need no action. A finding can be unreachable, unexploitable, or already mitigated by a runtime control. Generic severity scores don’t tell you which resources a threat actor can actually reach, so a critical score on a dev-only utility looks the same as a medium score on a service one step away from a payments database. Previously, confirming whether a finding was exploitable took hours of manual investigation, and shipping a fix with confidence took days of coordination across security, infrastructure, and application teams, because the blast radius of a change is hard to assess without business context. To close that gap, Continuum proves which findings are exploitable and bounds the risk of each fix it proposes.

Continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment. For AWS, you set up a collector in the account and Region where your code runs. The collector gathers resource details such as AWS Config resources and network configuration so Continuum can judge whether a vulnerability is reachable over the network and what a threat actor could reach from it. From this graph, Continuum learns which systems are business-critical, who owns them, how services depend on one another, and which data each one touches. It uses that picture to identify your highest-value systems, such as customer data stores, payment pipelines, and authentication services, and then ranks each resulting issue by how close its attack path runs to those systems.

Continuum analyzes each finding against your code and its environment context and assigns an evidence level, such as a verdict proven by static analysis of the vulnerable code path. For findings it can reproduce, Continuum runs the exploit in an isolated sandbox and attaches proof-of-concept code with the reproduction steps. It produces the attack path, the supporting source analysis, and a blast radius assessment instead of a risk score alone. It also evaluates whether your existing defenses would detect and stop the validated path.

For each confirmed issue, Continuum generates a fix (a code patch, a dependency upgrade, or a configuration change) and opens it as a pull request in your connected repository, ready to review. Every fix requires human approval: you review and merge the pull request, so the final decision stays with your team. In the future, you will be able to build confidence in specific remediation classes and let Continuum apply those fixes automatically once its confidence gates pass, such as test coverage, scope bounds, and historical success rate.

AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities in actionTo show how this works, I open AWS Continuum in the console and go to Code vulnerabilities. Before I can review issues, I set up an environment. I connect a code source, either a GitHub integration or an Amazon S3 bucket, and then create an environment that scans it on a schedule I choose. An Amazon S3 source has a couple of prerequisites: the bucket sits in the same account and AWS Region where I turn on AWS Continuum, and I grant access through an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that AWS Continuum assumes. I can optionally add AWS infrastructure context by setting up an AWS Continuum collector in the account and Region where my code runs and authorizing my environment to use it. For the full requirements and steps, see the AWS Continuum User Guide.

The Overview page brings these pieces together in one place, showing my Code integrations, the Environments built on them, and the status of any AWS collector that supplies AWS resource context.

I open one of my environments. The Issues tab lists validated, prioritized issues rather than raw scanner output, each with a severity, a status, and the time it was created. I choose one of the issues.

The Overview rates it High severity, with the status Completed and the remediation already Delivered to GitHub. The Risk assessment explains why. Continuum rates its Exploitability as Exploitable, with an evidence level of Static proven and a validation run status of Completed. Likelihood is High, since the service is reachable from an attacker, requires no authentication, and needs no user interaction. Impact is Moderate, which means an attacker gains the ability to modify business data, with a blast radius reaching other users in the same tenant. A Proof section includes the source analysis behind the verdict.

The Remediation section shows a fix already delivered as a pull request in GitHub, changing four files, with 50 lines added and 24 removed across the cart service. Continuum opens the fix as a pull request titled Continuum fix, and I choose View pull request to open it in GitHub. The console is explicit that a generated patch does not mean the issue is fixed. I still review and merge it, which keeps the final decision with my team. A Contributing findings section lists the specific scanner finding this issue was built from.

The pull request description carries the same risk assessment, remediation summary, and proof from the console, so whoever reviews it in GitHub sees the evidence without leaving their workflow.

The Findings tab lists the raw scanner findings across the environment, the evidence that issues are built from.

The Scans tab shows the history of each scan with its status, origin, and request and completion times, and I use Configure scan frequency to change the cadence or Queue scan to run one on demand. The Configuration tab is where I manage the environment: the code and context sources it reads from, its code integrations, environment settings such as whether Continuum creates remediation patches, and the AWS collectors it uses for AWS context.

In a single workflow, I work through the validated issues in priority order with each scan, reviewing the evidence and scope behind each one before I approve and merge the fixes I trust. Every fix waits for my approval, so the backlog keeps shrinking while my team keeps control of what ships.

Now available AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is available today in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon) Regions. For pricing, visit the pricing page.

To learn more, visit the AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities product page and the User Guide. Give it a try in the AWS Continuum console today, and send us feedback through your usual AWS Support contacts.

Esra Kayabali is a Principal Solutions Architect at AWS, specializing in analytics, including data warehousing, data lakes, big data analytics, batch and real-time data streaming, and data integration. She has more than ten years of software development and solution architecture experience. She is passionate about collaborative learning, knowledge sharing, and guiding community in their cloud technologies journey.

#9981. Gatwick drop-off customers' personal data exposed in supplier breach

AutoPay login and vehicle records affected, alongside limited payment information and customer service emails

London Gatwick Airport has warned customers that a breach of its drop-off payment service exposed personal information and, in limited cases, payment records.

A notification email seen by The Register identifies the affected system as AutoPay, operated by ParkPark and used by Gatwick's drop-off zone manager, Times24 UK Limited.

AutoPay lets drivers register their vehicle and payment details in advance so drop-off charges are collected automatically.

Gatwick told us it was unable to provide details about how many customers were affected by the breach, or how far back the affected records go.

The email said most affected customers would have only some of the listed data exposed. The could include names, home addresses, cities, postcodes, contact details, and AutoPay login credentials such as email addresses and bcrypt-hashed passwords were affected.

Other records implicated in the breach include details of vehicles linked to AutoPay accounts, those vehicles' entry and exit times at Times24-managed parking locations, and vehicle registrations.

The email also states that payment records, including amounts, card types, card expiry dates, payment references, transaction statuses, transaction IDs, and drop-off locations and times were affected, but a Gatwick spokesperson said this applied only to "very limited cases."

Again, in a minority of cases, "some limited emails between the customer service team and customers" were also exposed, the email stated.

Gatwick said Times24 "immediately suspended" AutoPay after detecting the intrusion. The service remains disabled while the investigation continues.

Airport officials are overseeing the response with outside cybersecurity specialists. Gatwick warned of possible disruption to its website but said flights were unaffected.

Customers can still use Gatwick's drop-off zones, although they'll have to use alternative payment methods, and all other airport services are still operating as usual.

The notification email urged customers to exercise caution when receiving communications from Gatwick, Times24, AutoPay, or ParkPark, especially those that ask for payment or bank details.

Times24, which operates across more than 200 car parks in the UK, did not immediately respond to our request for more information.

Dray Agha, senior manager at Huntress's tactical response division, warned that criminals could use the data for convincing scams long after news coverage of the breach has faded.

"The real damage often comes after the breach," he said. "Criminals rarely use stolen data straight away; they'll wait until the headlines fade, then send a text about a 'parking fine' or an email offering a 'refund' that references a real booking. Even partial card details add a layer of credibility that makes people far more likely to hand over the rest.

"Gatwick customers should assume any unexpected message about their parking could be a scam, check directly with the airport, and keep a close eye on their bank statements over the coming months." ®

#9979. AWS Weekly Roundup: Amazon Polly Generative engine, TorchNeuron for Trainium, and more (October 26, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

A few weeks ago I presented to a small group of commercial and technology leaders from Brazilian agribusiness at the AWS office in São Paulo. My talk ran through where generative AI fits across the different stages of an agribusiness operation, and the point I kept returning to is that the markets we call traditional are exactly the ones where keeping up with this technology decides who ends up ahead of the curve. Nobody there was arguing about whether AI belongs in agriculture. The questions were about delivery: who receives the output, in which language, on which device, often while driving between farms. That is why a launch I might otherwise have filed under routine leads my list this week. The Amazon Polly Generative engine upgrade added 14 new voices, two of them in Brazilian Portuguese. When your user has both hands on a steering wheel, the interface is a voice.

Presenting “GenAI no Agronegócio Brasileiro” at the AWS office in São Paulo.

The rest of the week had a sharper edge. The biggest launch is a security service built on the premise that the gap between a vulnerability being disclosed and a vulnerability being exploited has effectively closed, and AWS published the honeypot evidence for exactly that in the same week. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available AWS Continuum reframes vulnerability management as an end-to-end job rather than a scanner that hands you a list. It builds a context graph from your repositories and your AWS environment, assigns each finding an evidence level, and reproduces exploitable findings in an isolated sandbox with proof-of-concept code so you see the issue rather than a severity label. It ranks issues by how close the attack path runs to business-critical systems, then opens the fix as a pull request. The control boundary matters: every remediation currently requires human approval, so you review and merge the pull request, with autonomous classes of fix gated behind confidence thresholds for the future.

The “why now” came from AWS’s own honeypots in the same week. Amazon Threat Intelligence found a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt in MadPot telemetry dated October 17, four days before CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were publicly disclosed, and on disclosure day proof-of-concept exploits were circulating around 02:00 UTC, roughly twelve hours before the embargo was due to lift at 14:00 UTC. The practical reading is direct: a patch window measured in days assumes a delay that no longer exists, and an investigation should start from the earliest known exploitation rather than from the disclosure date. AWS also published the AWS WAF mitigations for the same CVEs. Continuum is available in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon).

Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway Amazon ECS Gateway splits the work of exposing a service between the people who own the network and the people who own the application. Platform teams define one gateway with the organization’s subnets, security groups, TLS certificates, listener settings, and AWS WAF web ACLs. Application teams opt in by adding a gateway connector to the service definition, and ECS gives them an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, listener rules, a target group, and a security group that admits traffic only from the Application Load Balancer.

The numbers make the economics clear: up to 25 services share a single ALB, ECS provisions the first ALB on first connect and removes ALBs when they are no longer needed, and a gateway can associate with up to 10,000 clusters, with five gateways per cluster. You can adopt it incrementally with UpdateService while your existing load balancer stays in place. Amazon ECS Gateway is available in all commercial Regions where Amazon ECS is available, at no additional charge.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches that caught my attention this week.

Amazon Polly delivers a major upgrade to its Generative engine – The Generative engine now runs a larger, more expressive catalog: 57 generative voices across 11 languages and 25 locales, with 14 new voices across 9 locales and Hindi and Finnish generally available for the first time. Two of the new voices are Brazilian Portuguese, Leo and Carolina. It is a drop-in upgrade, so the voice names, the same SynthesizeSpeech call, and the price all stay the same while the output gets more natural.

AWS announces TorchNeuron: native PyTorch support for AWS Trainium (public beta) – TorchNeuron is an open source PyTorch backend that lets you run your model on Trainium by switching to .to(‘neuron’), a configuration change instead of a rewrite, with eager execution and torch.compile intact. It integrates with the Neuron Kernel Interface for custom operators, and it works on Trainium2 and Trainium3 instances. If you want the bigger picture on why hardware choice should not lock in your software, the AWS Insights piece on that theme is a good companion read, and the release lands alongside AWS Neuron 2.33.

New ways to customize models with Amazon SageMaker AI, without managing GPUs – Training sessions are now generally available, giving you control of the post-training loop, including custom loss functions and reward signals, while SageMaker AI handles GPU allocation, distributed execution, fault recovery, and checkpoint storage. You pay for the tokens SageMaker AI processes, and the meter stops while your reward function scores a batch. There is a full technical walkthrough, the training session APIs, and new support for Muse Glimmer, Qwen 3.8, and Ministral 3.

Structured outputs for Claude models available on Amazon Bedrock – You can now get schema-compliant JSON back from any Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock, across both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints, without custom parsing, retry logic, or post-processing. That makes jobs like pulling every required field from a financial report, parsing clinical notes, or routing support tickets by intent far more reliable to automate.

Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey now supports online migration with zero downtime – You can migrate self-managed Valkey or Redis OSS on Amazon EC2 into ElastiCache Serverless with zero downtime, meaning zero errors returned to the client during the move, measured the way the ElastiCache SLA measures availability. You prepare the migration, start the data sync, then choose a manual or automatic cutover, with no third-party replication tools. It is available in all commercial Regions, the China Regions, and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

Other AWS news Here are some additional projects and posts that you might find interesting.

Discover tools at runtime with AWS Agent Registry – AWS Agent Registry is a managed catalog for MCP servers, agents, and agent skills, so an orchestrator can search approved capabilities at runtime instead of compiling every tool in at build time. This walkthrough shows the discover, instantiate, and execute loop in a working sample, with search results that return connection metadata but never invocation credentials.

Tokenomics for coding agents: benchmark cost and quality on your own code – Coding assistants replay a growing transcript on every turn, so their cost math is nothing like ordinary inference. This post gives you open source tooling to measure model, harness, and hosting choices on your own repositories and build a cost-and-quality frontier you own, with sample results where routing came out 44.7 percent cheaper for 4.8 percent lower mean quality.

How U.S. Bank migrated 119 TB from Oracle Exadata to Amazon RDS for Oracle – U.S. Bank moved four Oracle Exadata databases totaling about 119 TB to Amazon RDS for Oracle using a config-driven pipeline built on Oracle XTTS, AWS DataSync, and Amazon EFS. The initial baseline copy finished in about 7 days with zero data loss and cutovers averaging roughly four hours per database, over a bandwidth-capped Direct Connect link.

Upcoming AWS events Mark your calendars for these upcoming events.

AWS re:Invent – AWS re:Invent runs November 30 to December 4 in Las Vegas, with more than 2,200 sessions. The session catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so now is the time to build your schedule.

AWS Community Days – AWS Community Day Brasil Norte takes place in Belém on October 31, closing out the 2026 Brazilian community season. Check the hub for events near you.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

Daniel Abib is a senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, focused on generative AI and Amazon Bedrock — and passionate about serverless. He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. A three-time Ironman finisher and four-time re:Invent speaker, he brings the same endurance mindset to building cloud solutions.

#9977. Amazon to flog motors in Britain, but Prime won't deliver

Hyundai leads 2027 rollout, with a showroom visit still required to finish the paperwork

Amazon is channeling its inner car salesman as it prepares to flog motors on the UK arm of its online tat bazaar.

Amazon Autos will launch in Britain in early 2027, its first expansion outside the US, where it debuted in December 2024. Customers can browse and reserve cars online before completing the purchase with a dealer.

Hoping it will be "a nice little earner," Amazon will let punters view real-time dealer inventory, prices, get an instant trade-in valuation, and connect with a local dealer to reserve a car, "all on Amazon."

In the US, the service now covers more than 150 cities and offers vehicles from 35 brands. Hyundai is the first announced UK carmaker partner, while dealer group Vertu Motors will list used vehicles. More brands and dealers are due to be confirmed before launch.

Hyundai's launch range will include electric, hybrid, and petrol models.

"Buying a car is one of the biggest purchases people make, and we think it should feel as simple and transparent as shopping for anything on Amazon," said Matt Nuffort, director of Amazon Autos International.

Of course, buying a car isn't quite like adding an air fryer or a memory stick to your basket. How does financing and checkout work for UK buyers? Customers will complete the purchase and paperwork at their chosen dealership.

Amazon is not offering financing itself, but buyers can explore financing options via the site, adjusting terms like deposit and duration to see how monthly payments change. Credit applications must be completed with the dealer.

In the US, buyers can submit a credit application through the platform, review terms and conditions, then sign electronic contracts online. They typically pay a deposit and visit the dealership to complete the remaining paperwork and pick up the vehicle.

Buyers shouldn't expect their new car to arrive in an enormous cardboard box with a smiley logo on it, or to be lowered onto their driveway by a giant Amazon delivery drone.

But given that one of the online retailer's flying delivery robots crashed into someone's garage after making a drop-off near Detroit last week, perhaps that's for the best.  ®

#9975. Qualcomm’s Oryon 3 Reaches the Top

Qualcomm’s laptop effort had humble beginnings. Their early Arm-based laptops used cell phone SoCs, and suffered from noticeably poor performance even against lower end Intel chips. But breaking into the PC market was going to be a marathon rather than a sprint, and Qualcomm has been persistent. Qualcomm created higher performance Snapdragon variants targeted at laptops, which became increasingly competent with each generation. Now, Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme can deliver CPU performance that challenges the best of its x86-64 competition. To deliver that performance, Qualcomm relies on the third generation of their in-house Oryon architecture, which I’ll call Oryon 3 for short.

The Snapdragon X2 Elite deploys Oryon 3 in both E-Core and P-Core variants, which Qualcomm confusingly calls “performance” and “prime” cores, respectively. P-Cores are the star of the show in the Snapdragon X2 Elite, where they provide both maximum single threaded performance while also providing the bulk of multithreaded throughput. That’s because Qualcomm has P-Cores outnumber their E-Cores by a factor of two, creating an inverted hybrid strategy compared to Intel’s. Thanks to this strategy, Qualcomm’s Oryon 3 P-Core variant shoulders most of the burden when it comes to Qualcomm’s PC market ambitions.

Oryon 3 takes on this burden by deploying an architecture with a strong resemblance to the first Oryon generation. Qualcomm technically has a second generation Oryon core, but only used it in phones. Their website also suggests it’s a very minor change over the first generation, so I’ll be treating first generation Oryon as Oryon 3’s direct predecessor.

Similarity to Oryon 1 is a good thing, because that gives Oryon 3 just about everything you could ask for from a 2026-era high performance design. From Oryon 1, Oryon 3 inherits an out-of-order window in excess of 600 micro-ops. Qualcomm has also carried forward a two-level cache setup that emphasizes speed over capacity. Compared to its predecessor, Oryon 3 takes things up a notch by pushing clock speeds to 5 GHz. It’s a huge 16% increase over the 4.3 GHz speed that Oryon 1 could reach, and is enough to offer a generational performance gain on its own. But Qualcomm doesn’t stop there. Oryon 3 increases core width to 9 micro-ops, up from 8 in its predecessor, and makes a number of improvements throughout the pipeline. Qualcomm brings SVE2 and SME support to the new core as well, keeping it up-to-date with the evolving aarch64 architecture and opening up new software optimization opportunities. In its role as a maximum performance architecture, Oryon 3 faces off against the likes of AMD’s Zen 5 and Intel’s Lion Cove. Arm’s Cortex X925 is another competitor, thanks to Nvidia’s laptop push with N1X.

Setting aside clock speed, Oryon 3’s headline architectural improvement is a core width increase from 8 to 9 ups. At the frontend, Qualcomm supports this by adding another decode slot. The fetch and decode pipeline otherwise looks mostly unchanged. Oryon 1 already had over-provisioned instruction cache bandwidth at 64 bytes per cycle, which is more than sufficient to feed a 8-wide or 9-wide aarch64 decoder. Qualcomm has also kept a 192 KB, 6-way instruction cache with hardware coherency, as well as a 256 entry 8-way instruction TLB. These large structures should help the core use its fastest instruction delivery path more often than its peers, which have smaller instruction caches and instruction TLBs. Impressively, Qualcomm managed to keep these large structures and add an extra decode slot while keeping a 13 cycle branch mispredict penalty. Clock speed increases often come with compromises like longer pipelines or smaller structures, but here Qualcomm is able to have their cake and eat it too.

Testing instruction bandwidth with a stream of NOPs validates the increased decoder width when the test loop fits within the instruction cache. Improvements continue at larger instruction footprints. Oryon 3 is able to sustain about 4 NOPs/cycle from L2, compared to 2 per cycle on Oryon 1. Qualcomm might have changed something with instruction prefetching from L2, or they might have widened datapaths between the instruction cache and L2. Whatever the case, Oryon 3 now matches the likes of AMD’s Zen 5 and Intel’s Lion Coves in terms of streaming code from L2, while boasting a much larger L2. AMD and Intel’s cores do have a L3 that provides more capacity than Qualcomm’s L2, but fetching code from that L3 will cause another drop in instruction throughput.

High core throughput places pressure on the branch predictor, which must follow the instruction stream fast enough to keep the core fed. Oryon 3 improves by expanding its predecessor’s ability to handle taken branches back-to-back. Oryon 1 could only do “zero-bubble” taken branches within a 8 KB instruction footprint. Oryon 3 can do so within a 2048 branch footprint, regardless of branch spacing and code footprint. Perhaps Qualcomm switched to using a fully decoupled 2048 entry BTB. Realistically, that means Oryon 3 should be able to do zero-bubble taken branches over a branch footprint 2x to 4x larger than its predecessor, considering typical branch spacing.

Compared to AMD and Intel’s latest cores, Qualcomm lacks any ability to handle more than one taken branch per cycle. Arm’s newer cores are also capable of doing two taken branches per cycle. I suspect AMD, Arm, and Intel decided that handling multiple taken branches per cycle became more profitable once their cores got wide enough, so seeing Qualcomm build a very wide core without that ability is surprising. Perhaps clock speed factors into that decision, because going from 4.3 to 5 GHz is a huge jump. If so, Qualcomm’s choice would be justified because a clock speed increase of that magnitude probably offers a larger performance increase than going for two taken branches per cycle. Of course, it’s impossible to know if branch predictor paths presented a timing challenge for Oryon.

For branches with dynamic taken/not-taken behavior, Oryon 3 has a 2-cycle conditional predictor. Testing with branches whose outcomes correlate with increasingly long history lengths shows an average 0.5 cycle increase in time per branch over an always- taken reference run, as long as the test stays within the conditional predictor’s capabilities. Because I randomly generate patterns so that each branch is taken roughly 50% of the time, a 0.5 cycle average penalty suggests Qualcomm only incurs the 2-cycle timing if the direction predictor disagrees with a base prediction. Direction prediction starts falling apart with more than 32K patterns in play, which is an improvement over the approximately 24K patterns that first generation Oryon could handle in this test.

For comparison, Zen 5’s conditional predictor can handle roughly 48K patterns before falling apart. Unlike Oryon 3, and unlike some older Zen generations, Zen 5 does not show an increase in branch latency compared to an always-taken pattern.

Indirect branches can go to multiple targets, and present another level of difficulty because the branch predictor has to select between previously seen targets, and must store more than one target per branch. Oryon 3 has a 2-cycle indirect predictor that can track 2048 indirect targets, matching its predecessor.

A single branch can jump to 256 targets without incurring a significant penalty. This could mean at least eight of the bits that Oryon 3 uses to index into its indirect target array are influenced by branch history.

A 50 entry return stack handles return predictions, just as on Oryon 1. However, testing shows that Oryon 3 can use all 50 entries before hitting a performance degradation. When call depth exceeds return stack capacity, Oryon 3 degrades gracefully rather than immediately taking a drastic penalty as Oryon 1 does. Oryon 1’s performance drop is heavy enough to suggest it’s mispredicting every return after the return stack overflows.

Perhaps Qualcomm implemented a new mechanism to keep a single overflow from messing up the entire return stack, and lets Oryon 3 only mispredict returns whose addresses get forced out on an overflow. Whatever this optimization is, it gives Oryon 3 return prediction behavior in-line with many other cores, including AMD’s Zen 5 and Intel’s Skymont. In capacity terms, AMD’s Zen 5 has a slightly larger 52 entry return stack.

Optimizations at the rename and allocate stage on Qualcomm’s big core are remarkably similar to those on its little core counterpart. Both cores can eliminate up to two register-to-register MOVs per cycle. They can also eliminate up to two add-immediate instructions, as long as their immediates sum to 255 or less. It’s slightly strange that Qualcomm has kept the same optimization capability even though the big core is more than twice as wide as its little core companion. That results in degraded microbenchmark figures when I chain dependent MOVs or add-immediate instructions without a break, because the wider core can get more of those instructions into the same rename group, which means the two-per-cycle restriction causes more missed optimization opportunities.

One of the best strategies in CPU architecture is to avoid changing something that isn’t broken. Oryon 3’s backend at a high level is basically identical to the one in its predecessor. That makes sense because if Oryon 1 encountered performance issues, they likely had little to do with its backend strategy. Qualcomm specifies a reorder buffer capacity of over 650 micro-ops for both Oryon 1 and Oryon 3. Microbenchmarking puts capacity at 675 micro-ops for Oryon 3, and 680 on Oryon 1. Register files and memory ordering queues see little to no movement in size as well.

Qualcomm’s choice to avoid major backend changes is justified, because Oryon 3’s backend structures remain competitively sized even against emerging competition like AMD’s Zen 6. Execution throughput also remains competitive. Oryon 3 does have slightly smaller memory ordering queues, and weaker vector execution throughput compared to its x86-64 counterparts. The latter comes down to having a smaller 128-bit vector width, which is especially a disadvantage against Zen 5. However, that should only affect a small minority of applications.

Even though Oryon 3’s backend is similar to its predecessor, there’s still plenty of change under the hood. Predication is a central feature in SVE2 and SME, so Oryon 3 gets a new 120 entry predicate register file. The predicate registers themselves only have to be 16 bits wide because of Oryon 3’s 128-bit vector length. But while the predicate register file doesn’t need a lot of storage, it does need to be hooked up to every major execution unit block. Predicate generation can happen from both the scalar and vector side. All four vector pipes and four load/store pipes support predication, meaning a lot of reads from the predicate register file.

New SVE2 and SME instructions also require changes to backend logic. SVE’s vector length agnostic design rides heavily on predicate generation instructions like those of the WHILE* variety (like WHILELO). Oryon 3 breaks WHILE* instructions into two micro-ops, which execute through the integer pipes to deliver a throughput of one WHILE* instruction per cycle. Predicate generation instructions that don’t require a GPR input, like PTRUE and CMPEQ, execute through two FP/vector pipes. Besides predication focused changes, SVE2 adds new math instructions like CDOT, meaning more execution unit functionality behind the vector/FP ports.

Like Oryon 1, Oryon 3 has a four-pipe load/store unit. Memory dependencies are handled by a robust store forwarding mechanism, which can do fast forwarding for all cases where a load overlaps a prior store. Oryon 3 is able to do that even when the load isn’t contained within the older store, meaning the load/store unit is able to combine data from both an in-flight store and data fetched from the L1 data cache. A dependent store+load pair has a latency of 6 cycles on the integer side, or 8 cycles on the vector/FP side. While Oryon 3 can’t do zero-latency store forwarding the way AMD’s Zen 5 and Intel’s Lion Cove can, the ability to avoid the 14 or 19 cycle penalty those cores take in partial overlap cases is quite nice. Arm’s Cortex X925 has the weakest store forwarding capabilities of the bunch, with no zero-cycle capability and a 12-13 cycle partial overlap penalty.

For independent accesses, Oryon 3 prefers 16B alignment for stores. Stores that cross a 16B boundary take a slight penalty, though curiously there’s no penalty for crossing a 64B cacheline boundary. Perhaps Oryon 3 has a special optimization for speeding up line-crossing stores. The same characteristics apply on the vector side.

SVE introduces scatter and gather functionality to the load/store unit, forcing it to handle possibly non-contiguous accesses from a single instruction. Testing with LD1W gathers (32-bit elements) achieves a core-wide throughput of 1-2 elements per cycle. Gathers therefore have lower throughput not just compared to contiguous loads, but also equivalent scalar loads. However, Oryon 3 has an optimization that allows repeated gather loads to the same address to execute at 4/cycle. Gathers therefore seem capable of using all four LSU pipes, and don’t go down a smaller subset of specialized pipes. However, the general case seems to rely on a complex flow that involves several micro-ops, resulting in lower throughput.

Dependent gathers have 14 cycle latency, which is acceptable for a non-contiguous load operation. Zen 5 handles vaguely equivalent AVX2 gathers with 19 cycle latency.

The load/store unit also has to translate program-visible virtual addresses to physical addresses that correspond to DRAM locations (or possibly MMIO). Qualcomm sized up the L1 DTLB from a 224 entry 7-way structure on Oryon 1, to a 256 entry 8-way one on Oryon 3. Perhaps Qualcomm always intended for the L1 DTLB to be 256 entries and 8-way set associative like the instruction-side L1 TLB, but couldn’t fit the last way into Oryon 1. A 256 entry L1 DTLB covers 1 MB of address space using 4 KB pages, which is a lot compared to the smaller L1 DTLBs on other designs. An 8K entry L2 TLB handles larger memory footprints, and serves both instruction and data accesses. The L2 TLB’s capacity is also impressive compared to the competition.

Comparing with Zen 5 can be complicated because AMD can opportunistically use a single TLB entry to cover up to four consecutive 4 KB pages, provided the translations have the same attributes and lead to contiguous physical pages. Zen 5 can cover more address space with its TLBs despite a lower entry count if it can make maximum use of that page coalescing capability, though I don’t have data on how effective that is in practice.

Testing with performance counters validates Qualcomm’s large TLB sizes. The core’s PMU indicates a rise in L1D TLB misses after 1 MB, when testing accesses with a 4 KB stride. L2 TLB misses rise after 32 MB, though they only sharply increase after 64 MB.

Qualcomm specifies 2-cycle latency for L2 TLB accesses, which would be incredible for a 8K entry L2 TLB. However, comparing L2 latency with 4 KB and 2 MB pages suggests that a L2 TLB hit costs at least an extra 6-7 cycles of latency.

Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X Elite used a two-level caching strategy that emphasizes speed over the ability to scale last level cache capacity and the number of cores served by each last level cache instance. For the Snapdragon X2 Elite Qualcomm upgraded the cache subsystem by increasing L2 capacity from 12 to 16 MB for the P-Core clusters. This cache capacity increase boosts the amount of cache a single core can allocate into. It also helps account for each cluster having six cores instead of four, though cache per core still drops slightly from 3 MB on Oryon 1 to 2.66 MB in Oryon 3.

16 MB of CPU-side last level cache isn’t large by 2026 standards. AMD’s standard Zen 5 configurations use 32 MB of L3 cache, while Intel’s Arrow Lake has 36 MB of L3. However, Qualcomm’s caching capacity is fine next to the 16 MB of L3 that AMD puts in their mainstream Strix Point mobile chip’s performance cluster, and Qualcomm makes their L2 fast for the capacity it provides. With 20-23 cycle latency depending on which core is making the access, Qualcomm’s L2 can return data faster than the 46 cycle latency that AMD’s optimization guide specifies for Zen 5’s L3. AMD’s 46 cycle figure seems to apply to configurations with 32 MB of L3, like on the Ryzen 9 9900X. A Zen 5 variant with 96 MB of L3 incurs several extra cycles of latency, showing how a triple level cache subsystem can enable last level cache capacity scaling because the core-private L2 cache reduces sensitivity to L3 latency. Intel’s Lion Cove is Oryon 3’s opposite with respect to caching strategy, with four cache levels to enable capacity/speed tradeoffs at L2 and L3.

20+ cycles of L2 latency is still high compared to 14 cycles on AMD’s Zen 5, so Oryon 3 uses a large 96 KB 6-way L1D. Unusually for a high frequency design, Oryon 3 achieves 3 cycle L1D latency. It’s an impressive achievement, because even Arm’s lower clocked Cortex X925 has 4 cycle latency to a smaller 64 KB L1D.

Oryon 3 only shows a slight latency increase as a pointer chasing test spills out of the L1D when using a 64 byte stride. Using a shorter stride increases the length of the pointer chasing chain, and more clearly shows the L1D’s capacity. Qualcomm seems to have a “correlated miss caching” (CMC) style prefetcher like many of Arm’s designs, which tracks when a cache miss for one address is likely to be followed by a second miss to another address. This type of prefetcher can follow pointer chasing chains and defeat latency testing if the tested chain falls within what the prefetcher can remember. If Qualcomm is doing this, and they do suggest it by indicating they have “pointer” prefetching algorithms, then the data above points to it being a L1D prefetcher.

Arm in contrast places their CMC prefetcher at L2, which lets it be more aggressive because a larger L2 cache is less sensitive to having some capacity wasted by useless prefetches. For example, the CMC prefetcher on Arm’s Cortex A78 is able to reduce latency across the Mediatek Genio 1200’s 2 MB L3 when testing with a 64B stride compared to a 8B stride (at least 32K pointer destination predictions compared to 8K on Oryon 3).

Oryon 3’s L1D can service four accesses per cycle, all four of which can be loads, and two of which can be stores. Compared to Zen 5 and Lion Cove, Oryon 3’s maximum load bandwidth is held back by its 128-bit vector width. However, Oryon 3 should remain very competitive when running code that can’t be well vectorized, or vectorized code that doesn’t scale to longer vector lengths.

L2 bandwidth is just under 32B/cycle for reads, in terms of how much data the core can get into registers. Qualcomm states that each core has a 64B/cycle datapath to L2. This can be validated by only accessing the first 128 bits of each 64B line, and treating that as loading the entire line because cache fills happen at 64B line granularity. Doing so gives about 48B/cycle of inferred L2 to L1D bandwidth. A read-modify-write pattern that creates equal traffic in both the L1D fill and writeback directions also reaches 48B/cycle.

I have a separate piece for more on the Snapdragon X2 Elite’s system level memory subsystem characteristics. Overall though, there’s a lot to like about Oryon 3’s memory subsystem. As long as you don’t benefit from having more than 16 MB of last level cache in each core cluster, Qualcomm’s cache setup should be more than a match for the triple level setups used by Intel, AMD, and other Arm cores.

Because running Linux on the Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme is complicated at the moment and difficult considering other time constraints (Chips and Cheese isn’t a job after all, and I have a real job to pay attention to), I tested SPEC CPU2026 using Windows Subsystem on Linux. I’m pinning the vmmemWSL process to a P-Core for predictability. Results show the Oryon 3 P-Core delivering desktop-level SPEC CPU2026 integer scores, even though it’s implemented in a laptop. That’s an impressive showing because desktop chips enjoy advantages like higher cache capacity, lower DRAM latency, and higher clock speeds. A comparison against a typical AMD or Intel mobile part would almost certainly hand Oryon 3 a victory rather than a tie.

Qualcomm does score slightly behind Zen 5 in SPEC’s floating point suite, but manages to stay ahead of Intel. Individual subtests show modest differences between the cores, though there are outliers. 706.stockfish for example hands Zen 5 a large win, because GCC 14.2.0 was able to vectorize a large part of it to use AVX-512.

However, AVX-512 does not give AMD a huge lead in SPEC’s floating point workloads. 749.fotonik3d and 765.roms execute a lot of AVX-512 instructions on Zen 5, but Oryon 3 is able to compensate with higher IPC. Both workloads tend to be more memory bound as well, reducing the benefit of AMD’s higher vector throughput.

Further performance analysis is difficult without more work because WSL only passes through a subset of performance monitoring events. However, there’s enough data to show that Qualcomm’s branch prediction accuracy is up there with the best. Overall branch prediction accuracy is actually a bit better than that of AMD’s Zen 5. Oryon 3 even scores a win in 723.llvm, which is SPEC CPU2026’s toughest branch prediction workload.

Performance counters also show the merit of Oryon 3’s large L1D. L1D cache sizes have remained stubbornly stagnant outside of Qualcomm (and Apple) cores. In 1998, AMD rolled out their Athlon core with a 64 KB L1 data cache. No current cores from AMD, Intel, or Arm have a larger L1D, and I don’t put Lion Cove’s 192 KB “level 1 of the level 1 cache” in the same category as a conventional L1D because of its higher latency.

Each vendor’s performance monitoring unit accounts for L1D misses differently, but the differences are large enough to show that Qualcomm can service a lot more requests out of its fastest cache level than Intel or AMD.

Third generation Oryon is a top-notch core with everything needed to succeed on a level playing field. Qualcomm has given their core a large out-of-order engine, is able to run it at 5 GHz, and feeds it with a competent branch predictor and a low latency cache setup. Oryon 3 joins Arm’s Cortex X925 in delivering desktop-level performance, and both Arm cores should be seen as serious pacing challenges for Intel and AMD.

Oryon 3 isn’t perfect of course. A wider SVE vector width could improve its situation relative to Zen 5 in vectorized workloads. Going to six vector/floating point pipes like in Arm’s Cortex X925 is an option too, though it may be difficult to pull off without regressing clock speeds. Qualcomm’s branch predictor could pick up some of the two taken branches per cycle goodness that’s now common on AMD, Arm, and Intel cores. Cache capacity could be an issue too, because a two-level cache setup forces a tightly coupled L2 design to meet latency requirements. That could make cache capacity difficult to scale.

All of those are areas for improvement, rather than significant weaknesses. SPEC scores for example show that a core doesn’t need to sustain two taken branches per cycle to be up there with the best, at least not in this generation. As for cache capacity, I can’t think of a consumer scenario where that makes a huge impact except for gaming. Games of course struggle with a binary translation issue, which is outside Qualcomm’s control.

Binary translation does bring up a problem for Oryon 3 though, because having a good core is only one piece of the puzzle. The software ecosystem that Qualcomm has to work with is a persistent sticking point, because while Windows on Arm has improved over the years, it’s still not as polished as a native x86-64 setup. Qualcomm has also struggled with Linux support. It’s a missed opportunity, because Linux is increasingly being seen as a strong alternative to Windows due to Windows 11’s misplaced priorities. Linux applications are also more likely to have aarch64 versions, minimising the importance of binary translation. Beyond the software ecosystem, Qualcomm’s laptop push faces headwinds because high DRAM costs push consumers to defer buying new devices. Laptops with soldered memory are especially vulnerable, because there’s no chance of buying a device with less memory with hopes of upgrading it later once prices drop. These challenges must be frustrating for hardware engineers who worked on Oryon 3, because they’ve built their most competitive CPU architecture yet, but need more puzzle pieces to fall into place.

I hope Qualcomm continues to run the marathon of breaking into the PC market, and the puzzle pieces line up soon to enable success. Oryon 3 is an excellent core. I’ve used the Zenbook A16 laptop sampled by Asus on a recent casual trip, and used it as a daily driver for a few weeks. The laptop is subjectively as fast as my desktop back at home, and shows just how far Qualcomm has gone. I want to see the people who worked on it rewarded for what they achieved. I also hope to see the Oryon line grow with future generations, and keep pushing the leading edge of single threaded performance.

Great to see Oryon scoring high . What GCC flags are used for this SPEC build?

#9974. AWS Weekly Roundup: GPT-6.1 Terra on Bedrock, Step Functions as agent tools, and more (November 2, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

The agentic launches that stayed with me last week had nothing to do with how capable a model is. They were about reach. AWS Step Functions, which already orchestrates over 220 AWS services, can now be handed to an agent as a tool, so workflows teams already trust became callable without a rewrite. In the same week, the AI blog published how one engagement platform exposed roughly 400 internal API operations the same way. Neither story involves rebuilding anything, only describing what exists and letting the agent find it.

The other thread was cost. OpenAI’s newest Terra model reached Amazon Bedrock priced well below the model beside it, and two post-quantum launches landed for a deadline nobody can put on a calendar yet. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

HeadlinesOpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock, and what interests me is where it sits rather than what it tops. Terra is the everyday-workload line of the GPT-6 family. In OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam evaluation it scored 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra, performed on par with GPT-6 Astra, and completed tasks more than three times faster than both. Those are OpenAI’s figures, not an independent test. The price is what I would check first: input and output tokens are at least 50% lower than GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra. It takes up to 1 million input tokens with text and image input, and you can reach it from the Bedrock APIs or ChatGPT Work and Codex.

AWS Step Functions workflows are now available as AI agent tools through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, which connects agents to tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The division of labor is the idea: the agent decides when to run a workflow and what input to pass; Step Functions runs each step exactly as you defined it. A support agent can trigger a refund, and the eligibility check, the manager approval, and the credit still happen in that order every time, because the ordering was never the model’s to improvise. Your existing Standard and Express workflows qualify as connector targets, and agents can also look up runs. It’s available in all Regions where AgentCore Gateway is, at standard rates.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:

AWS Key Management Service now supports ML-KEM for post-quantum key encapsulation – You can now establish a shared secret with a post-quantum algorithm using AWS KMS keys, with private keys in FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated HSMs. All three NIST FIPS 203 parameter sets are supported through Encapsulate, which produces a random 32-byte shared secret and its ciphertext, and Decapsulate, which recovers it. The threat is harvest now, decrypt later: an adversary records today’s key exchange and recovers the secret once quantum computers are powerful enough. It’s available everywhere KMS runs except the Middle East (UAE and Bahrain) and China Regions. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL added post-quantum TLS key exchange the same week, on versions 18 and higher.

AWS IAM Identity Center now supports cross-Region trusted identity propagation – You can now carry a user’s identity with their request to AWS services in another Region. This removes a genuine architectural constraint: trusted identity propagation used to require every service accessing that identity to sit in the same Region, which left two unappealing options, broad IAM roles that cannot distinguish individual users, or consolidating all your services into a single Region. Now the identity travels with the request automatically, so you grant access by user and group membership and audit who accessed what. It’s available at no additional cost everywhere IAM Identity Center runs.

Amazon ECS now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS) – You can now run multiple Amazon ECS tasks concurrently on a single NVIDIA GPU, the practical answer to work that only ever uses a fraction of one, like small-model inference and multi-model serving. You declare the GPU memory each container needs and can optionally cap its share of GPU compute, and ECS places tasks on GPUs with available capacity as your services scale, with no code changes. It works on ECS Managed Instances and ECS on Amazon EC2, and on Managed Instances it watches the MPS control daemon and replaces the instance if it turns unhealthy. It’s available in all commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

AWS Lambda supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading for Lambda Managed Instances – You can now have AWS Lambda fetch only the files needed at each stage of startup instead of pulling a whole container image first, which AWS puts at up to 70% off container startup time. You create a SOCI index, push it to Amazon ECR, point the image URI at the indexed tag, and Lambda detects it automatically. The technique also reached Amazon SageMaker AI training and processing jobs, with benchmarks: lazy loading held at 3 to 11 seconds regardless of image size, against a median 3 minutes 42 seconds for a 13.2 GB image, a range they report as 8x to 46x.

Amazon EKS Auto Mode now supports Kubernetes Gateway API – You can now declare how traffic reaches your applications with Gateway and HTTPRoute resources on Amazon EKS without installing a separate controller, and EKS Auto Mode provisions and manages the underlying AWS load balancing infrastructure. You get HTTP and gRPC routing, cross-namespace routing, weighted traffic splitting, header-based routing, and automatic TLS certificate discovery through AWS Certificate Manager. Existing Ingress workloads keep working alongside them, so this is additive rather than a migration. Gateway API support is included with EKS Auto Mode; standard load balancing charges apply.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:

How Nubank automated disaster recovery with the AWS DevOps Agent – Nubank serves more than 140 million customers across Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia, and classifies over 300 business flows as critical, each tested on a regulator’s schedule. Nubank reports that handing evidence collection and report writing to the AWS DevOps Agent cut a test cycle from about 4.3 hours to roughly 40 minutes, and quadrupled flow coverage in 2026 to more than 160. One execution terminated more than 900 EKS instances under synthetic traffic with AWS Fault Injection Service, producing the evidence its regulator needed.

How MoEngage turned over 400 APIs into agent tools with AgentCore Gateway – Roughly 400 internal REST API operations, built by 25 teams, sitting in private VPCs across seven Regions, with tenant identity that could never become a parameter the model gets to set. MoEngage estimates the managed path saved about six months of platform engineering. The detail worth stealing: a full tool listing would have crossed 20,000 tokens per connection, so agents search for tools by describing a task instead of receiving the catalog.

Reducing petabyte-scale S3 storage costs with evidence-based lifecycle rules – The hard part isn’t deciding to act, it’s knowing which data has gone cold and where it can safely live. This uses S3 Storage Lens groups and Storage Class Analysis to prove access patterns before moving anything. In the engagement described, 5.8 PB of logs in Amazon S3 Standard at approximately $241,000 per month showed an access ratio below 0.1% past 90 days, and a 90-day transition to Glacier Instant Retrieval cut the bill by roughly 70%, a figure the author ties to that workload.

Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events:

AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4, with more than 2,200 sessions. The event catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so register and claim your spots before they fill up.

AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders. The 2026 season is winding down as re:Invent approaches, so check the hub for what’s still on.

Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

Daniel Abib is a senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, focused on generative AI and Amazon Bedrock — and passionate about serverless. He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. A three-time Ironman finisher and four-time re:Invent speaker, he brings the same endurance mindset to building cloud solutions.

#9971. Microsoft 365 Backup stretches recovery window to ten years

Recovery windows of up to ten years are now available in Microsoft 365 Backup for OneDrive and SharePoint, up from a previous maximum of two.

The change took effect on October 31, though Exchange remains capped at two years.

Administrators can select recovery windows of three months, six months, or any whole number of years from one to ten. Microsoft's list price is $0.15 per GiB per month of protected content. Extended windows can increase costs by keeping deleted data billable for longer.

Switching to a longer recovery window will also not make backups for that period magically available. So no nostalgic trips back to 2016.

Wider recovery windows may appeal to organizations that need access to older data, but backups are not a substitute for compliance retention and archiving. Recovery after a breach or ransomware attack is also critical, particularly getting back to a healthy state before any malware seeped into files.

Microsoft says backups are physically redundant and geographically replicated while respecting the tenant's data residency requirements.

Full OneDrive account and SharePoint site restores offer recovery points every ten minutes for the most recent two weeks, then weekly points through the configured window, up to ten years.

Individual file and folder recovery is limited to recovery points from the most recent 14 days, regardless of the configured window.

Restore remains free, which is handy since regular testing is a vital part of any disaster recovery plan.

The arrival of a ten-year recovery window is good for enterprises that need it and have deep enough pockets. However, it is important to keep in mind that being able to configure a longer recovery window doesn't constitute a disaster recovery plan in itself and may be overkill in many instances.

Microsoft notes: "The existing one-year default recovery window remains unchanged. Longer recovery windows must be configured on the applicable backup policies."

The company also recommends that users "review your organization's SharePoint and OneDrive backup requirements to determine whether longer recovery windows are needed."

A decade of recovery history could be valuable. It also means a decade of data to account for when setting budgets, access controls, and retention policies. ®
