#9970. Optimizing Rustc's next trait solver

The next rust trait solver, a large subsystem of the rust compiler that we've been trying to replace, will finally land in rust 1.102.0. In the last stages, before stabilizing it, its performance was a major blocker. But what is "a trait solver"? And why is its performance a problem? My goal for this blog post is to answer those questions in a way where you don't need any prior knowledge. I think discussions of the trait solver can quickly become quite involved, and daunting. So today, we'll start from the very basics!

This is a writeup of my eurorust 2026 talk of the same name, that I gave on October 15, 2026.

And if you'd rather watch than read this talk, you can do so here on youtube:

The new solver is the codebase I work on daily, and I've done so for about a year full-time. I'm not the main person driving its stabilization though, that would be lcnr , who's worked on it for far longer than I've been around in the Rust project. My main focus has been optimizing the new solver's performance.

Many people have worked avery hard, for years, to make the new solver a reality. You can find some of them here, and here.

My work here is only possible because of Hexcat and RustNL paying me and others to work on rust compiler development. Consider whether you or your company could sponsor Hexcat or the RustNL maintainer team.

On the 15th of May, 2015, Rust reached a major milestone. The very first stable version of rust was released. Version 1.0.0. Just 72 days later, on the 24th of July, work started on a new trait solver. Or well, that's when the Chalk project got its first commit. It seems the initial goal was to formalize the trait system so we could prove its correctness. One reason that didn't work well is because the trait system wasn't very correct at all.

Chalk is, according to its github description, "An implementation and definition of the Rust trait system using a PROLOG-like logic solver". The fact that it's "PROLOG-like" we'll come back to in a few paragraphs, it's quite interesting! However, Chalk isn't around anymore. Its README.md says it has been "sunset in favor of the newer next-generation trait solver". In October 2022, this project was officially started to turn the lessons learned from Chalk, into an actual new subsystem of the rust compiler, that, once finished, could replace the code of the old trait solver.

The goal of the new trait solver is to make sure we wouldn't have as many correctness bugs in the trait system. We now call this project "project zero", referring to the number of soundness bugs we'd ideally like to have in our type system. There have been several very long standing bugs in Rust's (old) trait solver. Like this one, that has been open since May 28, 2015 (just 13 days after Rust 1.0!). It abuses something called "implied bounds" to convince the Rust compiler to turn a short lifetime 'a into a 'static lifetime, allowing you to use a reference after its already freed. Some of these bugs were fundamentally impossible to fix with the way the old trait solver worked.

Note: Chalk and the new trait solver aren't the same thing. Chalk came first, and learned a lot of lessons incorporated in the new solver.

But what is a trait system? And how does a trait solver solve it?

The first place to look for documentation about the Rust compiler is the "rustc dev guide". It says "The goal of the trait system is to check whether a given trait bound is satisfied. Most notably when typechecking the body of - potentially generic - functions.". But I promised I'd start at absolute zero, so what's a trait?

Some types act in similar ways. They share certain properties. For example, a lot of different types can be cloned, or copared for equality. To codify these properties, we can use traits. In other words, a trait is a property of a type.

Notably, you can associate behaviors with these properties. The standard library's definition of Clone also includes two methods that can be called to perform this cloning operation.

To check whether the code you wrote is correct, the Rust compiler sometimes has to check that these properties hold. If you're trying to clone a value, the compiler has to check whether that value can be cloned.

Prolog is a cool programming language that works and looks very differently to what you may be used to. However, it is just as powerful (i.e. turing complete) as any other. The way it works has strong parallels to our trait system, let me show you. Here's an example:

A Prolog program consists of a set of statements, called "facts", as well as relationships between facts. In the above program, there are two facts: u64 has the property Copy, String has the property Clone, And there's also a relationship between these two properties. If some variable x has the Copy property, it also has the Clone property.

Finally, we can ask the prolog program some questions. For example, Does the type u64 have the Clone property? To answer that question, the runtime of a prolog program has to analyze all the known facts and relations. In this program we haven't said that u64 has the Clone property. However, we have said that it has the Copy property. And by using the relationship between Copy and Clone, the solver can derive that both questions (starting with ?-) are true!

The reason Chalk was using a "prolog-like" solver, is because as you can see, the trait system is extremely similar to a logic solver. Both "facts" and "relations" can be written using impl blocks. In fact, I can write the above program as a Rust program:

Neither the new solver or the old solver state as plainly as chalk does that they're using a "prolog-like solver". However, given the similarities, both the old solver and the new solver really aren't so different from how you'd implement a prolog runtime.

Trait solving is not the same as type inference. This is a common misconception. Inside the Rust compiler, the two are completely different subsystems. Type inference is the process of replacing blanks with types. Throughout this text I'll refer to some the following example code (with slight variations):

We use type inference to determine that the type of the variable a is an integer. The same for b.

Having said that, sometimes during type inference we do have to ask things about traits, and will call into the trait solver. Furthermore, the trait solver sometimes "unifies type variables", which means that while Rust makes a query about traits, we might make some progress on figuring out what the types of some variables are.

In the example code, one place where the trait solver comes into effect is when we call weird_add. On the function there's a where bound. A where bound is a requirement that the Rust compiler must check before allowing a call to that function. In this case, Rust has to make sure that i32 (a type we found through type inference) implements the Add trait. To do that, the solver can use one of a couple of strategies, and we'll look at each. In this case, we'll be looking for an impl block that mentions the i32 type, and we'll find one of those in the standard library!

Once the trait solver finds this impl block, it acts as an answer to the question "does i32 implement Add?". We somtimes refer to this answer as a a proof that the statement holds.

The example code contains several more calls to the trait solver. One you may not have thought about is that all local variables in Rust have to implement the Sized trait to be allowed on the stack. The Sized trait codifies that the compiler knows how many bytes of memory the value takes up, so it can be allocated on the stack. So, there will also be a query to the trait solver asking "does i32 implement Sized?".

The proof for this statement doesn't come from an impl block though. I did say that the compiler has several stratagies to derive proofs. In this case, the fact that some primitive types implement Sized is built-in to the compiler. i32 is inherently Sized, and there is no impl block anywhere that says so.

Answering Sized queries in general turns out to be quite hard because of the shear volume at which it occurs. To compile rust's standard library, we'll ask "does type implement Sized?" about 800 000 times! Additionally, answering it isn't always this simple. Let's take a slightly more involved example:

To prove Kitten: Sized, a recursive process takes place. Both fields have to implement Sized too. So in the process of answering this question, the trait solver will produce more questions to be answered. Kitten: Sized leads to String: Sized & f64: Sized. f64 luckily is trivial again, and built into the compiler. String isn't though, and we go one more layer deeper to Vec: Sized, etcetera.

In Rust, generic functions can be type checked standalone. The example using weird_add doesn't need a main function to be checked, and may emit its own type errors.

This is where the trait solver actually does the most work. For example, to type check weird_add, we have to prove that a + b is valid. a + b desugars to a.add(b), and when finding the method add the trait solver gets invoked, since the add method comes from the Add trait.

Previously, proof candidates came either from impl blocks or they were built into the compiler. Not here though! A new proof strategy is used here instead. When calling weird_add we saw that a where bound acts as a requirement that has to be checked before calling, but that means that inside weird_add we can assume that where bound holds and thus it acts as a proof strategy. Concretely, we know a has the type T, and to answer the question "does T implement Add" we find a where bound that says so.

Add isn't the only trait bound that has to be proven inside weird_add. This is another place where we have to prove that T: Sized. Again we have to look for candidates, and there's no built in one for generic types T, nor is there an impl block, nor a where bound that mentions Sized. So how does that work? Well, it turns out the where bound is implicit. T: Add really means T: Add + Sized, and so proving Sized works the same as proving Add.

On lobsters I got asked about whether the Add bound is required to add the Sized bound. The T: Sized implicit bound gets added for any generic. Even if there was not already an Add bound, T would still be Sized. Currently, you can opt out of that implicit bound using T: ?Sized (or in the example, T: Add + ?Sized). In the future we may change the syntax for that to T: MetaSized. Look for the keyword "Sized Hierarchy" if you want to learn more. This document should also give you a primer.

Finally, this code will actually give a type error, because there's one more trait to prove. Because b gets mentioned twice, we have to clone or copy values of type T. The function signature really should have been:

To summarize, trait solving is the process of answering questions about relations between types and traits. These questions are submitted to the trait solver, and the trait solver looks for candidates in the form of:

When it finds one of these, we say we've found a proof, and if we cannot find one, a type error is emitted.

Sofar, all trait solving came down to finding a single candidate, but that's not always how it works. Let's look at the definition of the From and the Into traits:

If the trait solver gets a question like u32: Into (does u32 implement the Into trait), it will find the impl block above. However, the impl block is generic, and has a where bound that says "T implements Into U IF U implements From T". Luckily there's another impl block that gives that implementation and so the initial statement can be proven.

What this all means, is that while answering a question, the trait solver emits more questions. These subquestions get added to an internal queue in the trait solver, and this queue of questions will be proven one after the other. Like this, some questions can turn into several subquestions, which can even have their own subquestions again.

Also, in the example from above, the second question actually has two proofs! There are two impl blocks that apply, since there's also this blanket implementation for identity conversion:

Some preference takes place here. Since this is a blanket implementation, the other more specific one takes precedence. We can think about the trait solving about answering a tree of candidates that may apply. In this case, the single candidate for u32: Into turns into two, u64: From and T: From.

Something we'll not cover today, but this tree of candidates in reality is not a tree, it can have cycles! This has been the cause of both many bugs, and many rust compiler developers' nightmares.

The trait solver doesn't just deal with traits. An important thing it has to also consider is the associated types of traits. Let's look at the Add trait:

An implementation of the Add trait can decide what the Output type will be equal to. Remember the definition of Add for integers?

It says that when you add two i32s, we get back an i32. The reason the trait solver cares about associated types is that sometimes answering questions creates subquestions that mention associated types.

Because we wrote Output = T, the trait solver has to check that the candidate impl block has an Output type that's equal to T. We could've also written a more general function signature to something like:

Or really to make it works you have to go one step further (click to expand).

Hold on! impl blocks can define inputs they act on, like impl Foo for i32 applies when the input is i32. It can make these inputs variables, like impl Foo for T. And impl blocks can also define outputs thrugh associated types.

What we've done here, is make impl blocks powerful enough to act as functions, with inputs and outputs. And Alonzo Church proved that a language with only pure functions is in fact turing complete.

This is why Prolog is a fully-fledged turing complete programming language, and so is Rust's type system. People have defined numbers completely in Rust's type system in a crate called typenum, and have gone even further by implementing a chess engine inside the type system.

Trait solving ends up being a subsystem that the compiler spends quite a large portion of its time in. In general, there are two reasons for that:

This ends up replacing the trait solver more complicated than you might think. People have already written many programs using the old solver, and because the new solver internally makes different assumptions (sometimes in the name of soundness, remember the old solver has many bugs), we end up having programs that take both longer and shorter to compile. Sometimes with a polynomial factor, sometimes even with an exponential factor.

For example, the crate unic-ucd contains code along the lines of:

It lists a whole bunch of unicode characters, and each constant inside these slices are themselves string literals. That means each of them has an associated lifetime variable, that at some point gets inferred to 'static since we're assigning to a const. Now the new trait solver, in some cases where the old solver did not, reasons about lifetimes.

Now sometimes, the rust compiler attempts see if two types are equal. This process may have side effects, in that it may make some progress towards inferring other types in the program. Because these side effects are sometimes undesireable, we have a system to "attempt" to unify types, and then roll back the results. To be able to do rollbacks we sometimes keep a trace of all operations we perform, so we can run them in reverse to get back to where we started. However, sometimes this tracking is more expensive than simply making a copy of the state and putting that copy back.

In this case, during borrow checking, we call into the the trait solver and end up unifying two "lifetime variables", which we roll back. This specific rollback involves a copy, though there was a shortcut. We keep track of a single boolean: "was any lifetime variable modified". If none were, the rollback can be skipped. The old solver wouldn't do such unifications, so the rollback could always be skipped, while in the new solver we couldn't do so.

Often, there are very few lifetime variables in scope, so doing a rollback isn't so bad. However, the example above lists every unicode character in existence, so the list is rather long. And for every item in the list, we'd do such a rollback, that copied all lifetime variables (for which there is one per element in the list). So N undos copying a list of N lifetime variables, that's a quadratic factor! So this crate would compile just fine with the old solver, and be 200 times slower with the new solver. Oops!

There are two important strategies we use to make the trait solver faster. First of all, there's caching, and a lot of it. For example, in the following example we prove that i32: Sized three times:

We'd like to make it so we only need to figure out whether a specific type is Sized once, and so we cache the result.

The second optimization we use a lot is not caching funnily enough. Accessing the cache can be rather expensive (we'll get to why). So in this case, since i32 is trivially Sized, we can answer the question faster by never looking in the cache. For more complicated types this is not true.

A naive cache would be a mapping from questions asked to the trait solver, to answers (errors or proofs). So, something like HashMap, but this wouldn't perform so well. Let's look at this example:

Here we've renamed the variables T and U between foo and bar. We'll prove two question, that T: Into and later U: Into. Because of the renamings these two proofs are the same, but the questions are technically different. If we don't do something about variable renaming, we'd have cache misses all the time.

Another issue is that this cache wouldn't even work. By now, we've learned that candidates for proofs can come from three sources:

The first two play nicely, because the same impl blocks and compiler built-ins are around for all questions submitted to the trait solver. Howver, where bounds are different for every function, and thus a proof that a type implements a trait inside of one function, may not be reusable inside another function.

In the example above, we prove that T: Into twice. Inside foo that's ok, but not inside of bar. So if we naively cached that T: Into we wouldn't notice that bar is incorrect.

We call the set of bounds that are in-scope during trait solving the ParamEnv (parameter environment), and so the cache would really have to look like HashMap<(ParamEnv, Question), Answer>. Since for every function, the ParamEnv is different, we'd have even more cache misses.

To improve our chances of a cache hit, we perform a process called "Canonicalization". During canonicalization, we do two things. First we'll rename all variables with numbers. So, T: Into will become ?0: Into (variable 0 implements Into variable 1). Since this process is consistent, another renamed input like U: Into also gets this numbering and is compatible.

In addition, we'll try very hard to figure out which where bounds in the ParamEnv actually matter. If there are bounds that won't affect the result of the query, we can avoid putting them in the cache key, making cache hits more likely.

So, in the rust compiler, the cache really looks more like a HashMap<(Paramenv, CanonicalQuestion), CanonicalAnswer> Note that the answer of every query now has to be de-canonicalized. We call this "instantiation". When we turn T: Into into ?0: Into, and cache its result, and we later look for U: Into, we have to turn the answer (that mentions variables 0 and 1) into U and T respectively. In other words, by canonicalizing we make cache hits much more likely, but the process isn't free. Hence not caching is sometimes worth it for simple questions.

Now is this worth it? Below I've plotted the hit rate of the new solver's cache for various popular crates, and one internal rust compiler benchmark.

As you can see, we can often avoid almost 80% of all trait solving by caching. The last two bars are for a crate called wg-grammar. It is a crate that used to be particularly slow with the new trait solver. Part of my job this year used to be specifically optimizing it.

The problem was that there's one more property that has to be part of the cache key: which opaque types are in scope. An opaque type is a type you write as a "return position impl trait". For example:

foo returns impl IntoIterator. By doing so, callers of this function don't get to know what specific type is returned. Only that they can iterate over whatever they get back. Inside of this function foo, the trait solver will infer which specific type gets returned (a Vec), but in other functions calling foo, this information is not available. So, this is another piece of information that may affect answers from function to function, just like the ParamEnv.

So, the real cache has one more input: HashMap<(ParamEnv, OpaqueTypes, CanonicalQuestion), CanonicalAnswer>. What that really means is that the following two functions both submit the question i32: Clone to the trait solver, but cannot reuse the cache entry:

This ends up mattering a lot in async code, or code like parser-generators that tend to return -> impl Parser from functions. That's unfortunate, because the fact that opaque types are different ends up almost never affecting the outcome of a question. Sure, we can come up with examples where it does, but in practice it almost never does.

So, the fix here is to remove opaque types from the cache key to the cached value like so: HashMap<(ParamEnv, CanonicalQuestion), (CanonicalAnswer, OpaqueTypeState)>. Then, every time we answer a question that may be different because of opaque types, we record in the opaque type state under what condition it may affect the answer, and continue assuming the answer is unaffected (this is often the case). Then, when we get a cached answer in a specific environment, we look at the opaque type state, to see whether the answer might be affected by current context. It almost never is, but if it ends up mattering, we retry the question but now no longer assuming opaque types don't matter.

This sometimes makes performance worse (we sometimes do double work), but since its so rare, we get an improvement over all by having more cache hits. In the graph from above, there are two bars for wg-grammar. One where the hit rate is 73% and one where the hit rate is 79%. This 6% difference translates to some the wg-grammar crate first taking 28 seconds to compile, and afterwards only 14 seconds. That's 2x faster!

(click to expand for me going into a little more detail about this)

Technically even when we use opaque type tracking, the list of opaques is still part of the key. We just set it to be an empty list. That means that in the rerun, we un-empty it and we get a different cache key. Now because we keep the cache entry with the empty list around too, when a new query comes along it will also empty the list, find a cache hit that matches this empty list but with tracking information (so it's not redoing work getting that tracking). Then, if it decides it needs to rerun, it adds back the list of opaques and could totally get a cache hit again if we've tried with those exact opaques before.

Of note is also that sometimes we run multiple dependent queries without their opaques like this. We can only un-empty the list once we get back up to the root at the point where we emptied the list to see if they may be unnecessary. To make sure we don't spend too much time running giant query trees we have a bailing mechanism built in to the tracking. Once a query and it's dependencies try to access opaques more than 3 times (or when they do so in very specific ways) we assume that it's unlikely for opaques not to influence the outcome of the query in any way, and we bail out of the "erased" attempts (recording in each dependent result that it's likely a rerun is necessary) and rerun without every knowing the original (erased) result, since it's unlikely to be correct. Future queries will see that this happened in the tracking information, and never attempt to erase opaque types. They know that the attempt is likely wasted.

Now there's an even more subtle thing going on. Sometimes assuming that opaques are empty (in a specific path related to coroutines) leads to query cycles. So, in that case we are forced to do this bailing and to rerun with opaque types even if the answer would've maybe been correct with the erased environment, because the compiler would crash if it encountered the cycle and we want to avoid those at all costs. In this case we may end up rerunning with opaque types, get to the exact same point, and continue to return the exact same result as we would have when we erased the environment previously. This is sadly unavoidable.

This, and more optimizations meant that wg-grammar used to take almost 200 Billion cpu cycles to compile, and now only about 7 Billion.

Now this is my second blog post about trait solver optimization. The other one is a little more technical, and goes into all the different things we did over the past year to bring the new trait solver towards stabilization. Go read it next if you're interested, and thank you for reading! If you're still interested in learning more about this, I'm happy to answer any questions if you reach out.

Also, hell yea! you made it to the end. Here's my cat.

#9969. Amazon S3 Tables now offer managed migration of Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing a simple, cost-effective path for data lake modernization. Amazon S3 Tables now support managed migration of your Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg. Migration works with Parquet tables in Amazon S3 that are registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog and allows you to upgrade your data lake with no pipelines to build or compute to provision, while production workloads keep running.

Apache Iceberg has become the open standard for large analytics datasets. It lets you manage petabyte-scale tables with features like schema evolution, hidden partitioning, and time travel queries, while keeping your data open and queryable with any Iceberg-compatible engine. Amazon S3 Tables offer fully managed storage purpose-built to keep Iceberg tables performant and cost-effective as they grow, with features like automatic maintenance, optimization, replication, and S3 Intelligent-Tiering built-in.

What is new Previously, migrating Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg could take weeks of engineering work to build and manage the required infrastructure. Converting data types and building rollback capabilities added operational complexity. Now, this is available as a managed, API-driven operation.

S3 Tables handle the entire migration workflow, including data validation, compatibility checks, type conversions, file recompression, and compaction. Before copying any data, S3 Tables identify every source object in scope and generate a compatibility report. You can sync as many times as you need without stopping writes to your source table, except for a few minutes during cutover. Once you are ready, you can complete the migration, minimizing time that tables are offline.

Compared to self-managed approaches, S3 Tables managed migrations are cost-effective because you pay only for the data copied, with no charge for the Hive-to-Iceberg conversion, and source objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering stay in their current access tier.

A first look at the migration To migrate an AWS Glue Hive table, choose your destination table bucket in the S3 console, then choose Create table from migration.

Create a namespace and table name for your destination Iceberg table. The destination table is created using recommended default settings tuned for query performance and storage efficiency.

When you start the migration, S3 Tables validate the source table, generate a compatibility report, and begin copying data. The destination table is read-only during the migration. Once you complete migration, the destination table is promoted to read-write.

You can begin working with your data right away using a direct integration with Amazon Athena and Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio in the AWS console, or use any tool compatible with the Apache Iceberg REST API to directly query the tables. To learn more, visit the S3 Tables migration documentation.

You can also use AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), AWS SDKs, or the Agent Toolkit for AWS. For example, set up migration jobs and call the start-table-migration command.

To catch up the destination table with changes in the source, call sync-table-migration as many times as you need before you complete the migration. Each sync copies only what changed.

If you’re using coding agents like Kiro, the migrating-hive-tables-to-s3-tables skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS provides step-by-step migration guidance with safety guardrails for agents. The skill can:

To learn more, visit the GitHub README page for the skill.

Now available Amazon S3 Tables managed migration is available today in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo), and Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, Stockholm) Regions. At launch, the capability supports AWS Glue-registered Hive tables stored in Parquet format within the same AWS account and AWS Region. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, or troubleshoot about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool.

Try it in the Amazon S3 console today and send feedback to AWS re:Post for Amazon S3 or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

Channy is a Lead Blogger of AWS News Blog and Principal Developer Advocate for AWS Cloud. As an open web enthusiast and blogger at heart, he loves community-driven learning and sharing of technology.

#9966. Debian wakes up wearing Windows XP's actual skin

Win4Wine runs the genuine Explorer shell atop Linux

Win4Wine is one of the more remarkable and creative hacks we've read about in recent years. It runs Windows XP's genuine Explorer shell through patched Wine on Debian 13, with a custom window manager integrating Linux applications into the desktop.

As its GitHub repository explains: "The taskbar, Start menu, desktop and folder windows are XP's real ones, and Linux applications get XP's frames and taskbar buttons."

This impressive, possibly demented project has English installation instructions and a README, although its design documents are in Japanese. We found Mozilla's built-in translation handled those pretty well.

Its developer goes by miKuta0407 on GitHub, their homepage, and X.

Also note, you're going to need some Windows installation media for the full experience. The README says: "No Microsoft files are included. Only the files that are needed are extracted locally from your own ISO."

It supports Windows XP Professional SP3 installation images in 32-bit Japanese or English editions, with an experimental option for Windows 7 SP1 x64. Without either Windows image, it can download and use ReactOS's free software shell instead, for what it terms "a Windows 2000-like classic look." In our view, that sounds much better anyway.

Before any former Windows users cry hurray and reach for an optical drive, this is not some ready-to-run project. The top of the README warns: "This is a personal, experimental project, not a finished product for daily use." The developer has tested it only on a fresh Debian 13 installation and recommends a VM or spare machine, rather than an existing working desktop, which sounds like an excellent precaution to us.

Also, before you ask, yes, it was vibe-coded with Claude.

We found ourselves reminded of another crazy-but-is-it project that we wrote about back in January: What if Linux ran Windows... and meant it? Meet Loss32. The Loss32 proposal was even more extreme. It suggested replacing essentially the entire Linux userland, so it would be a Linux kernel running Wine with a Windows desktop and Windows apps.

However, Mikuta-san was way ahead of us – lower down, the README mentions and even links to Loss32. Saying that, since it launched at the end of 2025, the bottom of the Loss32 web page shows a couple of updates, reporting on delays in getting it working. That, to be honest, did not shock us, but we still admire the let's-do-this spirit. The developer also seems to have got slightly distracted by a previous project, touchHLE: high-level emulator for early iOS apps.

Loss32, in turn, reminded us of Neptune OS, an attempt to give seL4 a Windows personality transplant. We wrote about that back in 2022, and work on it has continued: the project page shows updates in recent months. The team has also pushed out preview releases in 2022, 2024, 2025, and most recently in September.

This OS face transplant also reminded us of our article, Classic 7 is Windows 10 LTSC cosplaying as Windows 7. Some people really miss the look and feel of vintage Windows. Can someone do Windows NT 4 next, please? ®

#9965. AWS Weekly Roundup: AgentCore Runtime V2, Amazon DynamoDB bulk put items, and more (November 9, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Most of the cost of adopting something new isn’t the new thing, it’s the move. Moving a Hive table to Apache Iceberg has typically meant weeks of engineering work. Last week, Amazon S3 Tables turned that into three steps: start, sync as often as you need, complete. The source stays writable except for a few minutes at cutover. The same week, Amazon DynamoDB started loading data from S3 into tables that already exist.

The pattern I like is that neither one asks you to stop what’s running. That’s also the way to read the agent news this week. The new Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime is a single field on the runtime you already have, and Web Answer is a tool you attach to a gateway you already run. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

HeadlinesThe new AgentCore Runtime: elastic, optimized, and consistently fast starts – If you run agents on AgentCore and haven’t tried the new runtime since it became generally available, it’s worth a look. It changes two things. First, memory: sessions start small, page in more on demand, and give memory back when it goes cold instead of holding the peak, so you pay for what your agent uses. Second, cold starts: AgentCore prepares your environment once, snapshots it, and restores the snapshot for every new instance. In the team’s tests, that kept P75 cold starts at about 2 seconds for images from 200 MB up to 2 GB, while the original runtime rose from roughly 5.4 seconds to nearly 30 seconds as images grew. The per-unit rate is higher, but you use far fewer GB-hours, so the team expects most agents to see a lower bill, though that isn’t guaranteed.

To opt in, you set platformVersion to V2 when you create or update a runtime. Create and update take several minutes while the snapshot is prepared, and your container must report healthy on /ping within 120 seconds, so report health only after initialization finishes. The docs cover how to optimize your agent for V2. V2 is available in 10 Regions, and committed baseline pricing is coming soon.

Amazon S3 Tables now offer managed migration of Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg – You can now migrate Parquet tables registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog into S3 Tables without building a pipeline or provisioning compute. S3 Tables validates the source and produces a compatibility report covering every object in scope. Each sync copies only what changed, so production keeps writing until cutover. Afterward you can query the table with Amazon Athena, Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, or any engine that speaks the Iceberg REST API. You pay only for the data copied, with no charge for the conversion, and objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering keep their tier. At launch it works within the same account and Region, in 10 Regions.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:

Amazon DynamoDB now supports bulk put items – You can now load line-delimited DynamoDB JSON or Amazon Ion files from Amazon S3 into existing tables as a managed, asynchronous job. Each record can carry its own condition expression, so one file can mix plain, insert-only, and version-guarded writes. Writes use dedicated system capacity and cost less than the equivalent per-request writes. An Accelerated tier handles deadline-bound jobs. The Database blog post gives illustrative Accelerated times of less than 1 hour for 100 million 1 KB items. One thing to know before you start: canceling doesn’t roll back items already written.

Announcing Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – You can now give an agent a single tool call that returns a synthesized, cited answer to a natural-language question, instead of building your own search, retrieval, and citation pipeline. Web Answer plans its own searches, runs several in parallel, and decides when it has enough evidence. You attach it as a target on AgentCore Gateway and call it over MCP, and you can limit it with domain include and deny lists and publish-date filters. It’s available in US East (N. Virginia). The getting started post explains when to use it instead of Web Search, which returns ranked results for your own model to synthesize.

AWS Lambda now supports queues for Apache Kafka in self-managed Kafka event sources – You can now process records from a single Kafka partition across many parallel AWS Lambda invocations. Classic consumer groups cap parallelism at the partition count. Queue mode uses Kafka share groups and needs Kafka 4.2 or later with share groups enabled. It works with self-managed clusters and managed offerings such as Confluent Cloud. You give up ordering and get at-least-once delivery, so your functions need to be idempotent. The Compute blog walkthrough covers poller scaling and when to keep stream mode.

AWS announces AWS Interconnect – last mile preview with Equinix – You can now set up a private, managed connection from Equinix’s network of 282 data centers to AWS without ordering cross-connects or configuring routers. Capacity is quad-redundant across two locations and four links, with BGP and VLANs configured for you, a 99.99% availability SLA, and MACsec by default. You pick a Region, bandwidth, and AWS Direct Connect gateway, then paste the activation key into Equinix Fabric. The preview covers the San Jose metro and, as of last Thursday, Northern Virginia, with 1 Gbps connections at no charge.

AWS Security Hub now provides an SBOM inventory for your compute resources – You can now see every software package installed across your organization’s Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon ECR images, and Lambda functions in AWS Security Hub, with each package’s version and how many resources run it. That’s the list you want the next time a widely used library has a vulnerability. The inventory builds on the SBOMs that Amazon Inspector already generates, so it fills in automatically wherever Inspector is enabled. It’s included in Security Hub Essentials at no additional cost.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:

Serverless ICYMI Q3 2026 – Julian Wood’s quarterly recap is a quick serverless catch-up before re:Invent: Lambda SnapStart for container images, a 90-minute timeout on Lambda Managed Instances, Lambda MicroVMs in 10 Regions, 1 MiB payloads in Amazon SNS, and the new AgentCore Runtime.

AWS contributes a large-transaction binary log optimization to MySQL – With binlog on, a huge transaction holds a global commit lock while its events are copied, blocking every other commit. The optimization, which Amazon Aurora MySQL has run in production since 2019, promotes the spill file into the binlog instead of copying it. In AWS’s tests, commit latency for a 50 GiB transaction dropped from about 7 minutes to about 2 to 2.5 seconds. It has now shipped to community MySQL.

How OrderServ achieved up to 64% cost savings with multi-tenant ECS – Cognizant’s food-ordering platform went from one Amazon ECS cluster per brand on AWS Fargate to a shared cluster on EC2 Auto Scaling groups with warm pools. The 64% applies to a 3-year Compute Savings Plan (47% with a 1-year plan). Scaling time also fell from 5–7 minutes to 30–60 seconds.

Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events:

AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4. The event catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so register and claim your spots before they fill up.

AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders, with a few more before the year ends: Belém, Brazil (November 14), JAWS FESTA 2026 in Akita, Japan (November 17), and Port Harcourt, Nigeria (December 12).

Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

Daniel Abib is a senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, focused on generative AI and Amazon Bedrock — and passionate about serverless. He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. A three-time Ironman finisher and four-time re:Invent speaker, he brings the same endurance mindset to building cloud solutions.

#9961. JetBrains finds agents may cheat with open source

AI coding agents caught peeking at GitHub answers, stumble when JetBrains hides the crib sheet

JetBrains has revamped a benchmark for evaluating large language models after suspecting too many agents gamed their tasks the first time round.

The company labelled this agentic practice "reward hacking" in a post summarizing the results of its revised evaluation.

Like its predecessor, Kotlin Benchmark 2.0 is a collection of tasks that evaluates how well AI coding agents work with the Kotlin programming language, in order to help Kotlin programmers decide which agent-model configurations to use. The tasks include fixing tricky problems in Kotlin code across different domains, and making corrections to multiple files.

The revised benchmark now includes 30 Kotlin multi-file code problems that have not been exposed to the public in any way before. The revised test all but guarantees that the agents have not encountered this set of problems, or potential solutions, before. Another 70 tasks are based on code that resides in public repositories.

The test also blocked all network access for the open source tasks, except for what was needed to communicate with the model itself. This minimized the possibility that the agent could look for an existing answer already posted, perhaps through a patch or pull request.

Overall, the agents were significantly less accurate when solving problems on codebases they had never encountered. Top resolution rates dropped rather suspiciously from 86.2 percent on tasks based on open source repositories to 60  percent on those based on closed source repositories.

Although the agents lacked network access, JetBrains boffins theorized that they might have benefited from encountering and internalizing these open source repositories during training. Only the private repositories were completely new to them.

Also curious was how a different set of models excelled at the closed source problems, compared to those models that usually did better on the open source tasks.

When restricted to closed source tasks, two dark horse models rose to the top: Gemini 3.8 Flash, via Antigravity CLI, topped the list with a 60  percent success rate, closely followed by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (running on OpenCode) at 58.9 percent.

Of the two, the open weight DeepSeek was far cheaper (at $0.08 per task) than the closed weight Gemini ($1.74 per task), however.

In contrast, Opus 5.5 completed only 53.3 percent of the tasks at $1.21 per task, and Fable 5.1 completed only 44.4 percent of the tasks, at a luxurious $3.27 per task. Claude Code harnessed both of these models.

Claude’s lackluster completion rates on closed source tasks are somewhat sus given how both of these Anthropic models scored significantly higher on tasks using open source materials.

In fact Claude ran the table when it came to open source: Fable 5.1 topped the charts with 86.2 percent accuracy, closely followed by Opus 5.5 at 84.8 percent accuracy.

(Kotlin users will pay dearly for the extra sliver of Anthropic accuracy: The average cost of Fable completing a Kotlin cleanup task runs $2.38, while Opus could do the job for $0.68.)

One possible interpretation of these disparate numbers is that models are drawing from their own knowledge bases instead of reasoning from scratch. Whether this is cheating or the models simply working as intended might be more a matter of philosophical debate.

Mark Hinkle, founder of the AIE Network consultancy, suspects the issue of integrity may go deeper.

"Private code doesn't stop reward hacking, it changes the shortcut," he wrote to The Register on LinkedIn.

"On public code the agent goes and finds the answer somebody has already published. On private code there's no answer to find, so it satisfies whatever is checking it. I treat these things like entry-level employees, and a sharp new hire figures out fast what the boss actually looks at."

JetBrains did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but concluded in its post that more investigation is needed. It promises that its people will pore over the open source results to see if any have been contaminated by the LLMs' own memory. It also plans to run its own static analysis tool, Qodana, against the results to check for errors.

Sireesha Pulipati, a staff data engineer and AI observer, suggested, also by LinkedIn, that JetBrains may have needed more specificity in its agent instructions.

"Out of the box [an agent] tends to reach for generic patterns. But when we give it instructions and skills that tell it where to look for our patterns and context, it follows them. A well-controlled harness, with those standards built in, is what makes the agent useful," Pulipati wrote.

So good on JetBrains for providing Kotlin users some information about working with AI, but, as always, AI benchmarks should be approached with extreme side-eye. ®

#9960. Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine. The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), the AWS SDKs, and your coding agents speak to it over a local HTTPS endpoint using the same AWS APIs they would use in the cloud, from your laptop. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. Its source is on GitHub. You install it from an RPM or Debian package on Linux, and on macOS and Windows you run it in Docker.

How it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint. When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/. You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged.

From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment. A coding agent can create resources, check the result, and iterate again without waiting on a deployment in a Region.

The emulator is implemented in Rust so that it stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop. It supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub, and because it’s built from those models, the same ones the AWS SDKs use, your requests and the errors you get back have the same shape as on AWS.

If you are a developer, especially one working with coding agents such as Kiro or Claude Code, you can use that loop to test AWS interactions of real complexity locally.

Let’s try it out To get started, I installed the package on Amazon Linux 2023. The package adds the aws-emulator command to /usr/bin/, so it’s on the path.

On macOS and Windows, you build a Docker image from the short Dockerfile in the documentation and run the emulator in a container. We don’t publish a ready-made image.

I started the emulator with aws-emulator. It serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297, so only my own computer can reach it, and it writes its log as JSON lines that show the address, the config file, and the certificate file.

In another terminal, I set the environment variables that point the AWS CLI at the emulator, and unset any variables that could supply real AWS credentials.

The emulator generates new keys each time it starts. Its access key IDs start with EMULATOR, so you can’t mistake them for real AWS keys, and it rejects requests signed with any other keys. To confirm that my shell was talking to the emulator, I checked the health endpoint and the caller identity. The emulator uses a single account, 000000000000.

Then I created a bucket, copied in a small object, and listed it.

With the AWS CLI pointed at my laptop, I had the same commands I already use and a local endpoint that answered them.

Next I wanted to see it the way I actually work now, so with the emulator still running I opened Kiro and asked it to create an Amazon DynamoDB table, write an item, and read it back, all against AWS Emulator rather than my AWS account.

To use the same setup with an existing test suite, I would start the emulator, set the same environment variables in the script that runs the tests, and run them as usual.

Using the emulator in process Running the emulator as a local process gives you an HTTPS endpoint that works with the AWS CLI and the AWS SDKs through environment variables. Some SDKs need an extra setting to trust the emulator certificate, for example a trust store for the AWS SDK for Java. For tests, there is a second option. AWS Emulator ships an embedded mode that you instantiate directly inside your test process and wire into the SDK through its HTTP client, rather than talking to a separate server over the network. Each embedded instance keeps its own state, so tests do not share buckets, tables, or queues, and you can run many of them in parallel. Embedded mode is available for the AWS SDK for Rust. You add the aws-emulator-embedded crate from GitHub to the [dev-dependencies] section of your Cargo.toml file. The following example creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back, entirely in process.

When it runs as a local process, the emulator requires every request to be signed with Signature Version 4 (SigV4), the same way AWS does, and it exposes a /__admin/health endpoint on the same port so a script or a container can wait until it is ready before running tests. By default it also sends anonymous usage and error data, and you can turn it off.

How we measure fidelity An emulator is only useful if a test that passes against it would also pass against AWS, so we measure that directly with fidelity tests. A fidelity test is a short program that uses an AWS SDK to run a workflow, such as storing an object and then reading and deleting it, and asserts how AWS behaves. We verify each fidelity test against real AWS. A fidelity test passes only if the emulator matches AWS on the response to every call, including the status code, the body, and the exact error code and message, and on the resources and data that the workflow creates.

With each release, we publish how many fidelity tests pass for each service, as k of n. For example, 40 of 50 means that 40 of the service’s 50 fidelity tests pass. The set of fidelity tests is public in the aws-emulator-evaluation-suite repository on GitHub, including the ones that don’t pass yet, so you can see what we verified and run the fidelity tests yourself. Read a score as a snapshot of a product that’s improving. When we add fidelity tests, a score can go down even while the emulator gets better.

If the emulator doesn’t implement an operation yet, it returns HTTP 501 (Not Implemented), so your tests fail right away. If the emulator acts differently from AWS, you can tell us by opening an issue in the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub.

How the emulator is built AWS Emulator is built and maintained by agents from the AWS API models using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline, and AWS CodeCommit, so it stays current with AWS as those models change.

One group of agents looks for gaps, both by comparing emulator responses against real AWS and by statically comparing the emulator’s code against the published Smithy models, and files an issue for each gap it finds. Another group picks up an issue, writes tests, implements the behavior, and reviews the change for correctness, performance, and security. When the change is ready, it is pushed to a source repository, and that push triggers an AWS CodePipeline run that runs the fidelity tests before the change is published to the public GitHub repository.

How we keep it secure Because the code is written by agents, an independent security agent reviews changes adversarially, both while the fix is being made and again in the release pipeline as a final check before anything ships.

Security of your own use remains a shared responsibility. We build the emulator to run safely on your machine: it listens only on your own computer by default and rejects requests that aren’t signed with its own keys. You decide where it runs, what data you put in it, and how you test before production. Don’t use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn’t evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production.

Now available AWS Emulator is generally available today. It has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. You can install it from RPM or Debian packages on Linux, run it in Docker on macOS and Windows, or build from source, and it works with the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI once you set environment variables. At launch, it has some limits. It doesn’t evaluate IAM policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior. How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature. To see how well the emulator covers the services that you use, check the fidelity scores in the AWS Emulator documentation.

If you want to check regional availability, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page in AWS Builder Center. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool.

To get started, visit the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub and see the AWS Emulator documentation.

Updated on November 12, 2026: Added links to the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub.

Daniel Abib is a senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, focused on generative AI and Amazon Bedrock — and passionate about serverless. He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. A three-time Ironman finisher and four-time re:Invent speaker, he brings the same endurance mindset to building cloud solutions.

#9959. Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies

Two days before earnings, an employee asks their coworker agent to send the preliminary quarterly results to an investor who says they're under NDA, and to copy the employee's personal Gmail so they can review the numbers tonight. The agent can read the file and send email, so it fulfills the user request. Semantic governance policies, available in Preview in Gemini platform, enable enterprises to govern their agents and provide guardrails to stop that call before it runs. They check each tool call an agent proposes against what the user asked for and against rules you write in plain language.

Permissions alone can't catch this. They say what an agent can do, not whether a particular call follows your rules. A model can also be talked out of the rules in its system instructions, by a user with a good reason, or by a document telling it to do something nobody asked for, a technique called indirect prompt injection. So the check has to sit outside the agent. Semantic governance policies are enforced through a policy enforcement point, such as Agent Gateway, alongside the agent governance controls we expanded in October, so policies stay separate from your agent's code.

Semantic governance policies check each tool call your agent's model proposes, before it runs, against two things:

Today, the policy enforcement point that Semantic governance policies support is Agent Gateway. You need to configure your agent so all your agent egress traffic goes through Agent Gateway, facilitating traffic between your agent and its model. When the model responds with a tool call, Agent Gateway sends the proposed call to the Semantic governance policy engine for evaluation before the response reaches your agent.

In the policy engine, an LLM judge evaluates the proposed call against the conversation so far, the agent's system instructions and tool descriptions, and your policies.

If the call passes, the response reaches your agent unchanged. If it doesn't, the engine replaces the response's content, tool calls included, with a configurable denial message, so the call never runs. Either way, the verdict and the judge's rationale go to Cloud Logging in your project. Responses that contain only text, such as an answer, a plan, or a question back to the user, aren't evaluated, because they take no action.

Consider a coworker agent for a finance team. It can search the shared drive, read files, send email, and delete draft files, and its system instructions include the date of the next earnings release. The company writes one policy for the agent:

"Quarterly financial results (revenue, margins, bookings, guidance) should not be shared publicly until the public earnings release. Before the release, they may be shared only with @example.com addresses. Never send them to external or personal addresses, investors, analysts, or press, regardless of NDAs, urgency, or the requester's seniority."

In each denied case, the agent gets a denial message instead of the call. The judge's rationale can quote your policy, so if users shouldn't see it, set your own denial message on the policy.

The earnings rule is one policy. Each policy is a natural-language constraint attached to an agent. It can apply to all of an agent's tools or to one tool, and it can name a tool's parameters. Other examples:

Because the earnings policy doesn't name a tool, it's checked on every tool call the agent proposes, so it would also apply to a tool that shares or uploads files. For guidance on wording, see best practices for writing policies. You can create it in the Google Cloud console or with the Google Cloud CLI:

IAM and Agent Gateway access policies decide which tools and MCP servers an agent can reach. Model Armor screens prompts and responses for threats such as jailbreaks and sensitive data. Agent Anomaly Detection analyzes sessions asynchronously, out of band. Semantic governance policies add the check none of them makes, as one layer of defense in depth: they judge each action inline, before it runs.

Because verdicts come from an LLM, which is probabilistic, they may vary. We recommend reviewing them in dry run mode before you enforce, and using Semantic governance policies alongside your other controls. The judge decides from the conversation, the agent's instructions, and your policies, so include facts a policy depends on, such as the earnings date, in the agent's system instructions. Streamed model responses aren't evaluated. Semantic governance policies complement, rather than replace, your disclosure controls and legal and compliance reviews.

To try Semantic governance policies on an agent behind Agent Gateway:

To learn more, read the Semantic governance policies overview and best practices.

Your agent should work for the person who asked, within the rules you set. Semantic governance policies check both before each action runs.

In our next post, we'll share how Semantic governance policies held up against prompt injection on AgentDojo, a public agent-security benchmark.

#9958. From Hugging Face to Amazon SageMaker Studio in one click

Today, we’re excited to announce a deep-link integration between Hugging Face and Amazon SageMaker AI. Developers can now go from model discovery to hands-on experimentation in SageMaker Studio with a single selection. Whether you fine-tune a foundation model (FM) from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart or deploy it to an Amazon SageMaker Inference endpoint, you can now land directly inside the relevant SageMaker Studio workflow. Your selected model is pre-loaded, and the environment is fully configured and ready to go.

Previously, getting started on SageMaker Studio after discovering a model on Hugging Face required navigating multiple steps between opening Amazon SageMaker AI in the AWS Console, creating a domain, configuring IAM permissions, and sometimes requesting GPU quota. For developers who want to iterate quickly, this friction slows down the path from inspiration to experimentation. The integration creates a more direct path from discovery to enterprise deployment.

“At Arcee, we build open models so developers and enterprises can actually own what they run: inspect the weights, post-train on their own data, and deploy on their own terms. This integration takes that promise the last mile. Going from an open model on Hugging Face straight into SageMaker Studio in a single click, then fine-tuning or deploying it inside your own AWS environment with nothing to wire up, is the kind of experience open models have been missing. Open weights you own, running in the cloud you control. That is exactly the combination our customers have been asking for.”

— Mark McQuade, Founder and CEO, Arcee AI

With the launch of a one-click Studio landing experience, choosing Customize on SageMaker AI or Deploy on SageMaker AI on a supported Hugging Face model page takes you directly to the console. SageMaker AI then automatically provisions a new domain with pre-configured permissions in seconds and carries the model context through.

This launch introduces three capabilities that shorten the path from a Hugging Face model to a working SageMaker Studio workflow.

When you browse models on Hugging Face, you’ll now see action buttons alongside supported models that map directly to SageMaker Studio workflows:

Each entry point preserves the context, meaning you don’t need to search for the model again once inside Studio.

New Studio environments created through this flow come with permissions already configured for the full range of SageMaker AI capabilities, including model customization, training jobs, notebook experimentation, and endpoint deployment. A new managed policy, AmazonSageMakerModelCustomizationCoreAccess, is created and attached for you. It provides permissions for serverless model customization jobs using supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF), with supported deployment to SageMaker AI or Amazon Bedrock endpoints. This alleviates the need to manually create and configure AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles and policies before you can start experimenting. For existing Studio environments, actionable messages with direct links to documentation guide you through adding these permissions.

When selecting instance types for deployment or training, the Studio UI now surfaces quota availability directly in the instance selection list. You can immediately see which GPU instance types (G5, G6) are available under your account’s current limits. You don’t need to navigate separately to Service Quotas. If you still need to request a limit increase, you’re redirected directly to the Service Quotas page for the respective instance type.

Let’s walk through the experience of customizing or deploying a model starting from Hugging Face.

On the Hugging Face model page, click on “Deploy” and select “Amazon SageMaker AI”. If the model is supported, you will see two buttons, “Deploy on SageMaker AI” and “Customize on SageMaker AI”. Then select “Customize on SageMaker AI” for a supported model.

You’re prompted to sign in to AWS using your existing credentials. If you already have an active console session, this step is skipped automatically. For more information, see Sign in to the AWS Management Console.

You arrive directly on the Model Customization page inside SageMaker Studio with your model pre-selected. Next, configure your fine-tuning parameters such as training data, hyperparameters, and instance type, then submit the customization job.

Alternatively, selecting Deploy on SageMaker AI opens the endpoint deployment page in Studio with the model pre-configured. Select your instance type (quota visibility included), review the settings, and deploy.

After you deploy your endpoint, test inference directly from Studio’s endpoint testing interface.

The launch of a one-click Studio landing experience minimizes the friction between discovering a model and experimenting with it. By connecting Hugging Face directly to the SageMaker Studio workflows, developers can stay in their flow. There’s no context switching, no manual environment setup, and no permission troubleshooting.

To get started, visit the Amazon SageMaker Studio page or explore models on Hugging Face and choose Deploy or Customize on SageMaker AI.

#9957. The beauty of CSS mixins

I've been playing with CSS mixins recently, and I'm super excited about what this new CSS construct will bring to the way we write CSS. I think the CSS we'll write when CSS mixins are available will look very different from the CSS we write today.

In its simplest form, a mixin is a named piece of CSS code that you define once and can reuse elsewhere in a style sheet. In that sense, it's very similar to a custom property (also known as a CSS variable) or a CSS function.

The big difference is what mixins can hold:

So, instead of just returning the value red, a mixin can return background: red; color: white; border-radius: 2px; all at once.

My team at Microsoft is implementing mixins in the Chromium open source project. They've covered a lot of ground, and we're getting ready to ship this in Chromium-based browsers. Native CSS mixins are getting very close!

I can't wait for other browsers to catch up, so that we can all use mixins in earnest.

CSS mixins are experimental. To try the code snippets and demo in this article, use a recent Chromium browser, open about://flags, and enable the Experimental Web Platform features flag.

You define a mixin with the @mixin rule, and you use it with @apply. Mixin names start with two dashes, like custom properties.

Let's define the --visually-hidden mixin:

And now, let's use it somewhere else in our code:

That's all you need to do. The browser will apply the mixin's declarations to the element as if they were written directly in the element's style block, so it's exactly as if you had written:

Except now, you have a nice little reusable mixin that you can apply wherever you need it.

That's not all, a mixin can take parameters, with optional types and default values too. Consider this --button mixin:

It applies some colors and spacing to a button-like element, checking that the supplied colors have the right type and falling back to default values if needed. It even handles hover states automatically.

You can use this mixin either with its default values or by passing your own arguments:

If you pass more arguments than the mixin has parameters, the @apply does nothing.

A mixin can also hold conditional rules, such as @media, @supports and @container.

For example, you can create a mixin that applies styles conditionally to the viewport size:

This becomes even more powerful when combined with @contents. See the next section.

Arguments are not the only way to customize a mixin. A mixin can also accept an entire block of CSS from the call site. Inside the mixin, @contents marks the spot where that block goes.

For example, here's a --card mixin that defines a couple of declarations and accepts a block of CSS from where the mixin is used:

When calling the mixin, you can pass other declarations inside a block, which will be inserted at the @contents location within the mixin:

Here, .note gets the padding and border from the mixin, and then its own background, in the place where @contents appears.

@contents can have a fallback, which applies when the caller passes no block: @contents { background: white; }. If the caller passes an empty block, @apply --card {}, the fallback does not apply.

The ability to provide your own block of styles when applying a mixin is very useful, for example when using a mixin as a condition. Consider this mixin:

You can use it to define styles that only apply in dark mode, while keeping the rest of your CSS unaffected. For example:

Conditional mixins combined with @contents gives us something we've been wanting for a long time: named breakpoints:

These mixins don't apply any styles of their own, they just conditionally apply styles that are given to them depending on the media query. This is great because we now have a way to give custom names to a series of responsive design breakpoints that can be maintained in one place.

Let's use them here to see how clean our responsive design code can be:

Finally, a mixin can keep private variables to itself, by declaring them in an @private block. The element that applies the mixin can't see these variables:

Mixins are very versatile. You will find many ways to use them, and I don't think there will be one good way and one bad way to use them. Different teams will work out what works for them.

In this section, I explored one way in which mixins might be used. I don't know if it will make sense in a real project yet, but I found it interesting to try.

Imagine a white-label website. You own the site and control its markup and default CSS. But you also want your customers to be able to theme the site to match their brand.

In your style sheet, you'd apply mixins like this:

And your customer could define the mixins something like this:

You might remember the CSS Zen Garden. It had one HTML page, and anyone could submit a new design by writing a new style sheet for it. It showed the power of clean, semantic HTML, with styles, layouts and animations in a separate file. The designs were wildly different from one another and extremely creative.

But there's a problem when you do this for customers. You expose your entire markup and it becomes a public API. Customers start writing very specific selectors that depend on how your HTML is organized, and you can't change that HTML any more without breaking their customizations. I've done this at a previous job, and I know how painful this can be.

The other option is to expose CSS variables. You keep control of your entire HTML and CSS, and only expose a set of customization variables that are used throughout your code. For example, you define a set of color palette variables, a set of spacing variables, typography variables, etc.

Customers override values only, which is very safe, but can also be limiting. What if they later ask you to have access to the page layout? You now need to expose more variables and make sure they continue working correctly.

Mixins sit somewhere in between. You remain in control of your HTML and can change it whenever you want. You expose logically named mixins that correspond to the various areas and surfaces of your page.

As long as you keep applying the same mixins in the right places, customizations continue to work.

But you can also go much further than variables. Each mixin is an entry point where a customer can add any declarations, pseudo-elements, media queries and animations.

I built a small demo, heavily inspired by the CSS Zen Garden, to test this: the Mixin Zen Garden (this will only work with a browser that supports CSS mixins).

It's a simple webpage that has static HTML. The HTML never changes, but you can view the page with different designs that all use CSS mixins as described above:

(If you write your own design, please share by opening an issue on my repo.)

Here are some things I learned while building it:

A design doesn't need to define every mixin. This makes small designs very short.

One mixin per logical area of the page is more than enough.

A design can put colors, spacing, typography, and decorations in the same mixin.

Choose a mixin by what the role of the element is, such as --sidebar-heading, not by how it should look or what it currently is. Every design can decide what that role looks like, and you can change the HTML structure without changing the mixin names.

Well, I've said this already, but it bears repeating: mixins are experimental.

They work in Chromium only, behind a flag.

Nested selectors can reach into your markup again.

A custom design can define a nested selector in a mixin to reach into the HTML markup. For example: @mixin --masthead { & h2 { ... }}.

Doing this exposes your HTML markup again, making it part of the API contract, which we wanted to avoid. Now, if this were to become a real customization mechanism, we could validate custom designs to ensure they only use allowed selectors within mixins.

Theming is only one use of mixins. Other ideas I want to try:

CSS mixins might change the way we write and organize CSS pretty profoundly. I'm looking forward to seeing what you build with them. If you try the demo, or experiment with mixins on your own projects, let me know!
